kaaba: The name Kaaba means cube in Arabic. In the pre-Islamic religions of Arabia many deities were represented by cubic stone carvings or cubic structures regarded as their abodes, with sacred zones around them. The Black Stone of the Kaaba has been compared to pre-Islamic stones called baetyls, often black and thought to be of meteoric origin. According to Islamic tradition, the Kaaba was rebuilt several times, notably by Ibrahim and his son Ismail. Scholars disagree about its standing before Islam: Christian J. Robin argues that it became prominent in the last decades of the 6th century, while Peter Webb argues that it largely played a local role in Western Arabia.

The Kaaba is a cuboid stone building at the centre of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, about 15 metres high, with sides of 12 and 10.5 metres. Inside, the floor is of marble and limestone, and the interior walls are clad with white marble halfway to the roof. Muslims consider it the House of God, and it determines the qibla, the direction of prayer. Early Muslims faced towards the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem before the direction changed to the Kaaba, which Muslims believe followed a Quranic revelation to Muhammad. Pilgrims circle it seven times anticlockwise in tawaf, which is required in both the hajj and the umrah.

Muhammad took part in the reconstruction of the Kaaba around 600 CE, after a fire and then a flood had weakened it. According to Ibn Ishaq, he settled a quarrel among the Meccan clans over who should set the Black Stone in place by having the elders raise it on a cloak and then setting it with his own hands.

The building was badly damaged by fire on 31 October 683 during the first siege of Mecca in the war between the Umayyads and 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, who rebuilt it. In 693 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan had al-Zubayr's building razed and rebuilt on the foundations laid by the Quraysh; its basic shape has not changed since. In 930 the Qarmatians sacked Mecca and took the Black Stone to al-Ahsa.
kabir: The years of Kabir's birth and death are uncertain, and some historians favour 1398–1448 while others favour 1440–1518. Followers hold that he came from Satloka and appeared on a lotus flower. A few accounts say that as an infant he was found at Lahartara Lake by a Muslim weaver named Niru and his wife Nima, who raised him. He is believed to have become a disciple of the Bhakti poet-saint Ramananda in Varanasi, and the Persian text Dabestan-e Mazaheb, the earliest known text with biographical information, calls him a Bairagi, a Vaishnava yogi, and a disciple of Ramanand. His family is believed to have lived at Kabir Chaura in Varanasi.

Kabir's couplets suggest that he was persecuted for his views while alive, and he was said to have been threatened by both Hindus and Muslims. Legends describe him as an underdog who triumphs in trials before a sultan or a Brahmin, but many scholars doubt them, pointing to the lack of corroborating evidence. When he died, Hindus and Muslims both claimed him.

Kabir composed his poems orally in Sadhukkadi, a mixed language drawing on Khadi boli, Braj, Bhojpuri, Marwari and Awadhi, in simple words. He and his followers called them bāṇīs, utterances, and they include songs and couplets such as the dohe and the sākhī, a word meaning witness. Collections attributed to him include the Kabir Bijak, the Sakhi Granth and the Kabir Granthawali, and his verses form the largest non-Sikh contribution to the Adi Granth. Except for the Adi Granth, the versions differ considerably, and the Bijak was first written down in the seventeenth century, so scholars debate which poems are authentic.

Kabir attacked what he regarded as the follies of Hinduism and Islam alike and questioned the need for any holy book. Linda Hess holds that he is falsely presented as a synthesizer of the two religions, since he declared his independence from both. He taught that God is within every person and urged people to drop the ego. The Kabir panth, a Sant Mat sect that recognises him as its founder, arose centuries after his death, over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and two temples to him stand in Varanasi, one maintained by Hindus and one by Muslims. Rabindranath Tagore's Songs of Kabir was first published in 1915.
kabuki: The history of kabuki is traced to 1603, when Izumo no Okuni, a former shrine maiden who may have served at Izumo-taisha, began performing with a troupe of young women in Kyoto. They gave a simple style of dance drama in pantomime on a makeshift stage in the dry bed of the Kamo River. In the earliest forms women played both men and women in comic playlets about ordinary life. Okuni was asked to perform before the Imperial Court, and rival troupes quickly formed.

The word is believed to derive from the verb kabuku, meaning to lean or to be out of the ordinary; the kabukimono were originally people bizarrely dressed, such as gangs of samurai. The characters for sing, dance and skill are ateji and do not reflect the etymology.

After women and young boys were banned from the stage in 1629, kabuki became the all-male form called yarō-kabuki. Male actors known as onnagata took over the women's roles, with young men preferred for their less obviously masculine appearance and higher voices. A kabuki stage has the hanamichi, or flower path, a walkway through the audience used for entrances and exits. Revolving stages and trap doors were introduced in the 18th century to produce sudden revelations and transformations.

Actors wear layered kimono in vibrant colours and the white oshiroi base. Kumadori make-up exaggerates facial lines into masks, with red for passion and heroism, blue or black for villainy, green for the supernatural and purple for nobility.

In the Genroku period the structure of the plays took the form still performed, and kabuki and the puppet theatre ningyō jōruri, later called bunraku, influenced each other. Chikamatsu Monzaemon was among the first professional kabuki playwrights; his The Love Suicides at Sonezaki, written for bunraku and adapted for kabuki, reportedly inspired copycat suicides and led to a government ban on plays about love suicides in 1723. The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō I is credited with the mie style of posing.  In 1842, under the Tenpō Reforms, the shogunate forced three theatres out of Edo into Asakusa and restricted the trade and socialising that went on in them.

After 1868 actors and playwrights worked to improve the reputation of kabuki, and the Emperor sponsored a performance on 21 April 1887. The occupying forces banned it briefly after the World War II, but the ban was rescinded by 1947. UNESCO inscribed it on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.
kabul: Kabul lies at an altitude of 1,791 m in a narrow valley of the Hindu Kush, along the Kabul River, in the eastern part of Afghanistan. South of the old city stand the ancient city walls and the Sher Darwaza mountain, and further east the ancient fortress of Bala Hissar. The city lies on the trade routes of Central Asia and South Asia and is traditionally seen as the meeting point between Tartary, Hindustan and Persia.

The origin of Kabul, who built it and when, is largely unknown, though it is believed to be over 3,500 years old. The Rigveda and the Avesta refer to the Kabul River and to a settlement called Kubha. Greek writers called it Kophen or Kophes. After Cyrus the Great annexed the Median Empire in 549 BCE, Kabul became part of the Achaemenid Empire and a centre of learning for Zoroastrianism, followed by Buddhism and Hinduism. An inscription on the tomb of Darius the Great lists it among the 29 countries of that empire.

After Alexander the Great annexed the Achaemenid Empire, the valley passed to the Seleucid Empire, which in 305 BCE ceded Gandhara, including the Kabul Valley, to the Maurya Empire. Trade flourished under Mauryan uniform weights and measures. Later empires that claimed Kabul include the Kushan, Ghaznavid, Ghorid and Timurid. In the 16th century the Mughal rulers used it as their summer capital, and it prospered.

Kabul became part of the Durrani Empire in 1747 and the capital of Afghanistan in 1776 under Timur Shah Durrani. British forces occupied it briefly in the First and Second Anglo-Afghan Wars. In the second half of the 20th century it was a stop on the hippie trail and was nicknamed the Paris of Central Asia. The Saur Revolution of 1978 and the Soviet intervention of 1979, which began a ten-year war, ended that period, and a civil war among mujahideen factions in the 1990s destroyed much of the city. The Taliban captured it in 1996.

Kabul is the capital and largest city of Afghanistan and has long been its political, cultural and economic centre. Its people speak mainly Dari and Pashto. Historical gardens and palaces include the Arg, Bagh-e Babur, Bagh-e Bala, Chihil Sutun, Darul Aman and Tajbeg.
kachin-state: Kachin State covers 89,041 square kilometres. It is bordered by China to the north and east, by Shan State to the south, and by Sagaing Region and Arunachal Pradesh in India to the west. Besides Myitkyina, its capital, its important towns include Bhamo, Mohnyin and Putao. The state holds Myanmar's highest mountain, Hkakabo Razi, at 5,889 metres, and a large inland lake, Indawgyi Lake. Its economy is predominantly agricultural, and its minerals include gold and jade. Hpakant is well known for its jade mines, and Bhamo is one of the border trading points with China.

The Nanzhao Kingdom controlled much of Upper Burma, including the area of the present state, and the Dali Kingdom afterwards administered the lands of the Kachin people. The Qing dynasty briefly controlled it during the Sino-Burmese War of 1760. The region was historically inhabited by many groups, among them the Rawang, Lisu, Jingpo and Zaiwa, and the term Kachin was given by the British in the colonial period. Traditional society rested on shifting hill agriculture, with political authority held by chieftains, and the people were animist. The British accepted the autonomy of the Kachin Hills, though their forces carried out expeditions against the Kachin in 1892 and 1896.

On 12 February 1947 Aung San reached the Panglong Agreement with the Shan, Kachin and Chin peoples, which envisioned a Kachin State. Burma became independent on 4 January 1948, and the state was formed the same year from the former civil districts of Bhamo and Myitkyina and the northern district of Puta-o. The northern frontier was not demarcated until the 1960s. After the military coup of 1962 Kachin forces, who had formed a significant part of the Burmese army, withdrew and formed the Kachin Independence Army. The state was virtually independent from the mid-1960s through 1994, when an army offensive seized the jade mines and a ceasefire was signed.

Kachin State had a population of 1,689,441 in the census of 2014. Its mountain hinterlands are mostly Kachin, while the railway corridor and southern valleys are mostly Shan and Bamar. Buddhists form the largest religious community, with a large Christian minority. Burmese and Jingpho are the lingua francas, and a railway links Myitkyina with Mandalay.
kaesong: Kaesong lies in the centre of Korea and is the southernmost city of North Korea, close to the border with South Korea and just north of Kanghwa Island. It covers 1,309 km2. The urban district is surrounded by Songak Mountain, 489 metres high, and Pongmyong mountain, and most of the area consists of low hills. The Imjin River runs along the north-eastern border and the Ryesong River along the western. About 55% of the area is forested, mostly pine, and the frost-free period of 180 days is the longest in North Korea. The earliest signs of habitation date from the Neolithic era.

The area lay in the realm of the Mahan confederacy and was known as Busogap under Goguryeo. Baekje held it for about 100 years until 475, and it became part of Silla in 555 as Song'ak-gun. As Silla declined in the late 9th century, Kaesong fell in 898 to Gung Ye, the founder of the short-lived state of Taebong, and in 919 became part of Goryeo under its founder Wang Geon, enthroned as Taejo of Goryeo, who made it the national capital. It was renamed Gaegyeong in 960. During the second conflict of the Goryeo-Khitan War in 1010 the palace and houses were almost burnt down.

In 1198 a slave named Manjŏk gathered other slaves outside the city, but Ch'oe Ch'ung-hŏn suppressed the plot. When Yi Song-gye overthrew Goryeo in 1392 and founded Joseon, the capital was moved to Hanyang, the modern Seoul. Under Japanese occupation from 1910 to 1945 the city was called Kaijō. After the Second World War it lay mostly south of the 38th parallel, and the Korean People's Army took it in the first days of the Korean War. Ceasefire negotiations began there on 10 July 1951, and the Armistice of 27 July 1953 left Kaesong under North Korean control, the only city to pass from South to North Korea as a result of the war.

Kaesong was named a special city in October 2019. Called Songdo while it was the capital of Goryeo, it prospered as a trading centre that produced Korean ginseng, and it is now North Korea's light industry centre. It is home to the World Heritage Site Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, which includes the remains of the Manwoldae palace, and the tombs of almost all the Goryeo kings, among them the reconstructed tomb of the founder Taejo. The Koryo Museum occupies the old Confucian academy of Songgyungwan, which began as the Gukjagam in 992. In 2009 the city had 192,578 inhabitants.
kagawa-prefecture: Kagawa occupies the northeast corner of Shikoku, a relatively narrow prefecture between the mountains of the island and the sea. The Sanuki Mountains run along its southern border with Tokushima Prefecture, and Ehime Prefecture lies to the west. Its coast on the Seto Inland Sea faces Okayama Prefecture on Honshu, to which it is joined by the Great Seto Bridge. It includes Shōdoshima, the second-largest island of the Seto Inland Sea. At 1,877 square kilometres it is the smallest prefecture of Japan by area. Takamatsu is its capital and largest city, and other major cities are Marugame, Mitoyo and Kan'onji.

Kagawa was formerly known as Sanuki Province. For a brief period between August 1876 and December 1888 it was made part of Ehime Prefecture. Yashima, a mountain in Takamatsu, was the battlefield of one of the best-known struggles between the Heike and Genji clans, the Battle of Yashima. Many of its towns were created after 1999 through mergers, as part of a national effort to reduce the number of small towns and villages.

The prefecture had a population of 949,358 in 2020, about 7.1 per cent lower than in the census of 2000. Sanuki udon is its best-known local food, and in 2008 there were over 700 udon restaurants in the prefecture. Kagawa was the first place in Japan to cultivate olives successfully, and it has produced olive goods since 1908. Sites include Ritsurin Garden and Takamatsu Castle in Takamatsu, Marugame Castle, the Konpira Shrine at Kotohira and the Kanamaruza Kabuki Theatre. The island of Naoshima holds several art museums, and Zentsūji and Yashima-ji are temples on the Shikoku Pilgrimage. Setonaikai National Park covers part of the coast.
kagera-river: The Kagera River, also called the Akagera River or the Alexandra Nile, forms part of the upper headwaters of the Nile and carries water from its most distant source. Its total length is 597 kilometres, measured from its source in Lake Rweru in Rwanda. The section named Kagera begins in Burundi, flowing out of that lake. It runs east along the borders of Rwanda with Burundi and Tanzania to a confluence with the Ruvubu River, close to the northernmost point of Lake Tanganyika. Its waters thus come from two major tributaries, the Nyabarongo of Rwanda, which feeds Lake Rweru, and the Ruvubu of Burundi. It is unknown which of the two is longer and so the ultimate source of the Nile.

From the confluence the Kagera flows north along the Rwanda-Tanzania border, over the Rusumo Falls, an important crossing point between the two countries, and through Akagera National Park. It then turns east along the Tanzania-Uganda border and empties into Lake Victoria in Uganda. It is the largest single inflow into the lake, contributing about 6.4 billion cubic metres of water a year, about 28 percent of the lake's outflow. The river gives its name to the Kagera Region of Tanzania and to Akagera National Park. Its basin is rich in fish, and because of its many waterfalls and rapids the sections of the basin are separated from one another.

Richard Kandt was the first European to reach the source of the Kagera, in 1898. The river has featured prominently in the histories of the countries it runs through, particularly Rwanda. In 1894 the German Gustav Adolf von Götzen crossed it at the Rusumo Falls, which marked the Rwandan colonial era, officially begun in 1899. In 1916, during the First World War, the Belgians defeated the Germans and entered Rwanda by the same route.

During the Rwandan genocide of 1994, thousands of Tutsis and Hutu political moderates were murdered on the river's banks, and the Kagera was used to dispose of the corpses. It carried the bodies into Lake Victoria, where they washed up in Uganda and created a serious health hazard, for which a state of emergency was declared in affected areas.
kagoshima: Kagoshima lies at the south-western tip of the island of Kyūshū, on the north-eastern part of the Satsuma Peninsula, and its area includes the whole of Sakurajima. It sits on the bay of the Aira Caldera beneath the stratovolcano Sakurajima and has been nicknamed the Naples of the Eastern world for its bay, warm climate and volcano. Ash from Sakurajima falls constantly on the city, and residents have developed ways of coping, such as schoolchildren wearing helmets against volcanic debris. The kanji of its name mean deer child island, but the source of the name is not clear.

Shimazu Ujihiza of the Shimazu clan moved into the area around 1340, and the city lies in ancient Satsuma Province, the centre of Shimazu territory from the late Kamakura period. Francis Xavier first reached Japan by landing at Kagoshima on 15 August 1549, on the coast of what is now Gionnosu. Kagoshima was a significant centre of Christian activity until bans were imposed in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

In the Edo period (1603–1868) Kagoshima became the seat of the Shimazu's Satsuma Domain, one of the most powerful and wealthiest domains in the country. Satsuma also controlled the semi-independent kingdom of Ryūkyū, and a special embassy building housed Ryūkyūan emissaries in the city. The domain was a centre of anti-Tokugawa sentiment.

In 1863 the British Royal Navy bombarded Kagoshima to punish the daimyō of Satsuma for the Namamugi Incident, the murder of a British merchant on the Tōkaidō the year before, for which the domain had refused to pay an indemnity. Many leaders of the Meiji Restoration and the Boshin War came from Satsuma. Nineteen young men of Satsuma broke the shogunate's ban on foreign travel and visited industrial sites in the United Kingdom, and a statue outside the train station honours them. Tōgō Heihachirō, who led the Grand Fleet of the Imperial Japanese Navy in the Russo-Japanese War, was born in Kagoshima.

The 1914 eruption of the volcano spread ash across the city with relatively little disruption. On the night of 17 June 1945 120 B-29 bombers dropped incendiary and cluster bombs, destroying 44.1 per cent of the built-up area; the city was targeted for its naval port and its position as a railway terminus. The municipality was founded on 1 April 1889, and on 1 November 2004 five neighbouring towns, among them Sakurajima, were merged into it.

Kagoshima is the capital of Kagoshima Prefecture and its largest city by a wide margin, with an estimated 583,966 people in 2024. Its economy centres on light manufacturing, tourism and commercial fishing, and the Kyushu Shinkansen linked it to Hakata Station in Fukuoka in 2011.
kagoshima-prefecture: Kagoshima Prefecture lies at the south-western tip of Kyushu, on the Satsuma and Ōsumi peninsulas, which are separated by Kagoshima Bay. It also includes a chain of islands, most importantly the Amami Islands, stretching a few hundred kilometres to the south-west, so that its coastline runs to 2,632 kilometres including 28 islands. Its position made it a gateway to Japan at various times in history. Active and dormant volcanoes are found across the prefecture. Sakurajima, which rises out of Kagoshima Bay opposite the city, sends up a steady trickle of smoke and ash. In its major eruption of 1914 the island mountain spilled enough material to become permanently joined to the mainland.

The prefecture corresponds to the ancient provinces of Ōsumi and Satsuma, together with the northern part of the Ryukyu Islands, known as Satsunan. Its territory formed the core of the Satsuma Domain, ruled from Kagoshima Castle, one of the most important domains of the Edo period and of the Meiji Restoration. The region played a key role in that Restoration through Saigō Takamori, and the city of Kagoshima was an important naval base in Japan's wars of the 20th century and the home of Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō. The Satsuma lord Shimazu Nariakira is said to have introduced the deep-fried fish cake satsuma-age from the Ryūkyū Kingdom.

The city of Kagoshima is the capital and largest city, and most of the economy is concentrated there and in the area of the former Satsuma Province. The eastern part, the former Ōsumi Province, is mostly rural. The prefecture has strong agricultural roots, and its best-known products include green tea, sweet potatoes, radishes, Berkshire pork and Black Wagyu beef. It has more than a hundred distilleries of shōchū, one of Japan's most traditional drinks. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency has facilities here, including the country's main launch site on Tanegashima. The people speak the distinctive Satsugū dialect, mutually unintelligible with standard Japanese, though most speakers know both.
kahramanmaras: Kahramanmaraş is the administrative centre of Kahramanmaraş Province in the Mediterranean region of Turkey. The city lies on a plain at the foot of Mount Ahır, 568 metres above sea level, and the Ceyhan River, which rises in the mountains around the Elbistan Plain, is its most important hydrological feature. Historically it was known as Marash, Maraş in Turkish, and Germanikeia in Greek. After 1973 Maraş was officially renamed Kahramanmaraş, adding kahraman, the Turkish word for heroic, to commemorate the Battle of Marash.

In the early Iron Age, from the late 11th century BCE to about 711 BCE, the city was the capital of the Syro-Hittite state of Gurgum, called the Kurkumaean city by its Luwian inhabitants and Marqas by the Assyrians. In 711 BCE Gurgum was annexed as an Assyrian province and named Marqas after its capital. The Romans called the city Germanicia Caesarea. In Byzantine times Germanikeia was the seat of an eparch, one of whom took part in the First Council of Nicea. It was lost to the Muslims in the 7th century, and under al-Mansur the whole Christian population of the Germanikeia valley was deported and resettled at Ramla in Palestine.

After the fall of the Armenian kingdoms in the 11th century, the city became a stronghold for exiled Armenians and the capital of the short-lived principality of Philaretos Brachamios. His successor, the Armenian general Tatoul, hosted the exhausted army of the First Crusade for four days. According to Matthew of Edessa, an earthquake destroyed the city on 29 November 1114 and killed 40,000 people.

It passed between the Danishmends, Seljuks and Crusaders, among them Tancred, who retook it in 1107. From 1337 to 1515 it was ruled by the Beylik of Dulkadir as vassals of the Mamluk Empire before being annexed to the Ottoman Empire. In 1525–6 it had 1,557 adult males, a total population of 7,500, all Muslims, and a substantial number of non-Muslims migrated there later, mainly in the 19th century.

In 1915 about 20,000 Armenians from Marash were deported. During the Turkish War of Independence the French army occupied Maraş, and in February 1920 Turkish nationalist forces regained control, followed by a massacre of the Armenian population. The official French report said the victims did not exceed 5,000. In December 1978 the Maraş Massacre of leftist Alevis, incited by the Grey Wolves, left more than 100 dead and contributed to the declaration of martial law and the 1980 coup.

Kahramanmaraş had 571,266 inhabitants in 2022 and is populated mostly by Turkish and Kurdish people, with a small Armenian population. The earthquakes of 6 February 2023 had their epicentre in Pazarcık and Elbistan in the province and destroyed much of the city.
kaifeng: In 361 BCE King Hui of Wei moved the Wei capital to Yi and built the city of Daliang. After Qin conquered Wei, Daliang was destroyed apart from a mid-sized market town renamed Junyi. Under the Han it was the capital of the Kingdom of Liang, ruled by Liu Wu, who restored the walls and made it a centre of music, art and gardens. The nearby Qifeng was renamed Kaifeng to avoid the naming taboo of Emperor Jing of Han. In the early 7th century, as Bianzhou, the city became a commercial hub when it was joined to the Grand Canal. During the Five Dynasties it was capital of four successive dynasties, and the Song made it their capital in 960 as Dongjing.

Under the Song, Kaifeng became the largest and most prosperous city in China, at the intersection of four major canals and surrounded by three rings of walls. It probably held between 600,000 and 700,000 people and is believed to have been the largest city in the world from 1013 to 1127. The memoir Dongjing Menghualu recalls its night and dawn markets, restaurants and theatres, and Zhang Zeduan's painting Along the River During the Qingming Festival depicts its bustle. The Iron Pagoda of Youguo Temple, built in 1049, is the oldest landmark of the city, and Su Song's astronomical clock tower used an escapement two hundred years before they appeared in the clockworks of Europe.

In 1127 the Jurchen Jin took the city and carried off the Song imperial family and officials; Zhao Gou escaped and the court never moved back. The Jin court itself moved to Kaifeng in 1214 to resist the Mongols, and in 1233 the city fell to them after a ten-month siege. Kaifeng was vulnerable on the Yellow River floodplain: five major floods struck between 1375 and 1416. In 1642 the Ming army flooded the city during a siege by rebels, and only 30,000 of its 370,000 people remained.

Kaifeng was rebuilt in 1662 and again after the flood of 1841, and was the capital of Henan until 1954. It is one of the Eight Ancient Capitals of China, having been the capital eight times, and has long been home to the Kaifeng Jews, the oldest Jewish community in China.
kairouan: Kairouan, in Arabic al-Qayrawān, takes its name from an Arabic word meaning military group or caravan, borrowed early from the Middle Persian kārawān. The city lies 50 km from the east coast of Tunisia, west of Sousse, 75 km from Monastir and 184 km from Tunis, and it has a hot semi-arid climate. It is the capital of the Kairouan Governorate. Its Great Mosque of Sidi-Uqba, one of the largest Islamic monuments in North Africa, covers more than 9,000 square metres.

The foundation dates to about 670, when the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi, acting for Caliph Mu'awiya, chose a site in dense forest as a military post for the conquest of the West. A Byzantine garrison town, Kamounia, had stood there before. Berber resistance continued under Kusaila, whose troops killed Uqba at Biskra about fifteen years later, and under a woman called Al-Kahina, who was killed and her army defeated in 702. A mass conversion of the Berbers to Islam followed.

Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab recaptured Kairouan at the end of the 8th century, and in 800 Caliph Harun ar-Rashid confirmed him as emir of Ifriqiya. His Aghlabid dynasty ruled until 909 and made Kairouan its capital. The Aghlabids built the great mosque and a university, which made the city a centre of Islamic learning.

After the Fatimids overthrew them in 909 they moved first to Raqqada and then to Al Mahdiyah, and Kairouan lost importance. The Zirids, ruling for the Fatimids after these had moved to Egypt, governed again from Kairouan, until in 1045 they declared independence and allegiance to Baghdad. As punishment the Fatimids sent the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym, who took and destroyed the city in 1057, and it never regained its former importance.
The city began to emerge from its ruins under the Hafsids in the 13th century. The French took it in 1881, after which non-Muslims could enter and live there, which they had been forbidden to do.

The old city and its monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. Besides the Great Mosque they include the Mosque of the Three Doors, founded in 866, and the Aghlabid basins of the 9th century, a water system with a storage capacity of 68,800 cubic metres. The city had about 187,000 inhabitants in 2014, and its Jewish community, a centre of Talmudic scholarship from the late 8th century to the early 11th, has left only a cemetery.
kakusthavarma: Kakusthavarma, also written Kakusthavarman, was a son of King Bhageerath, the third ruler of the Kadamba dynasty. When his father died the throne passed to his elder brother Raghu, and Kakusthavarma became Yuvaraja, or crown prince. As heir apparent he held a court of his own, perhaps at Palashika, the present-day Halasi, from where he is known to have issued land grants. In due course he succeeded his brother as king.

His reign is noted above all for its marriage alliances. The marriage of one daughter, read as a marriage into the imperial Gupta family, is counted the most important. It is also likely that another daughter married the Vakataka prince Narendrasena: Vakataka records describe Narendrasena's wife, Ajjhitabhattarika, as a princess of the Kuntala country, which probably corresponds to the Kadamba kingdom. Through such ties the Kadambas stood in close diplomatic relations with the great royal houses of India. The Talagunda and Halmidi inscriptions praise the king as a formidable warrior.

He appears also to have been a builder and a patron of both secular architecture and religious causes. He is described as owning numerous palaces adorned with gopuras. The Talagunda pillar inscription of his son Santivarma records that he had a great water tank made near a Shiva temple at which Satakarni and other kings of the past had worshipped. His own leanings seem to have been Jain: his grant at Halasi opens with an invocation to Jinendra, the lord of the Jinas, and he probably patronised a Jain temple there.

On his death the kingdom appears to have been divided among his descendants. One son, Santivarma, succeeded him at Banavasi and ruled the northern part of the realm. Another, Krishnavarma I, seems to have founded a junior branch of the dynasty at Triparvatha, in the south. The height of Kadamba power under Kakusthavarma was therefore followed by a kingdom held in two lines.
kalamata: Kalamata is the second most populous city of the Peloponnese after Patras, and the capital and chief port of Messenia. It lies on the Nedon River at the head of the Messenian Gulf. The modern name probably comes from a church title, the Virgin Mary with beautiful eyes, or else from the older name Kalamai, meaning reeds. The city occupies the site of ancient Pharae, mentioned by Homer.

Kalamata is first mentioned with its modern name in the 10th-century Life of St. Nikon. The medieval town lay inland, at the foot of Mount Taygetos, and prospered in the 11th and 12th centuries as capital of the fertile Messenian plain. After the Fourth Crusade it was conquered in 1205 by the Frankish lords William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin and became part of the Principality of Achaea, the centre of the Villehardouins' patrimony. Prince William II of Villehardouin was born and died there. It came under the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea only in 1428.

The Ottomans occupied Kalamata in 1481. In 1659 the Venetian commander Francesco Morosini took it, plundered it and carried off its able-bodied men to row in the Venetian galleys. He returned in 1685 at the start of the Morean War, and Venice ruled it as part of the Kingdom of the Morea until the Ottomans reoccupied it in the war of 1715.

Kalamata was the first city taken by the Greeks in the Greek War of Independence. On 23 March 1821 revolutionary forces under Theodoros Kolokotronis, Petros Mavromichalis and Papaflessas occupied it. In 1825 the Ottoman officer Ibrahim Pasha destroyed the city. It was rebuilt in independent Greece and became one of the most important ports of the Mediterranean. It was liberated on 9 September 1944, and an earthquake in 1986 killed 20 people.

Kalamata is known for the Kalamatianos dance, black Kalamata olives and olive oil, and exports raisins and olives. The 2021 census recorded 58,816 inhabitants in the city proper. Its sights include the Villehardouin castle, the Church of the Holy Apostles, where Mavromichalis declared the revolt of 1821, and the cathedral of the Ypapanti, consecrated in 1873. It is the seat of the Metropolitan Bishop of Messenia.
kalevala: The Kalevala is a 19th-century compilation of epic poetry by Elias Lönnrot, drawn from Finnish, Karelian and Ingrian folklore and mythology. Before the 18th century this runic song was common throughout Finland and Karelia, but it began to disappear in western Finland as European rhymed poetry spread. The nationalist and linguist Carl Axel Gottlund hoped for a Finnish epic in the manner of the Iliad, Ossian and the Nibelungenlied that would stir national feeling. Lönnrot, a physician, botanist and linguist, was district health officer of Kainuu from 1833 and made eleven field trips in fifteen years.

The work opens with the Finnish creation myth. The Earth is made from the shards of the egg of a sotka bird, and the first man, Väinämöinen, is born to Ilmatar, the Holy Spirit of the Heaven. Väinämöinen is a shamanistic hero with a magical power of song, associated with the kantele. The smith Ilmarinen forged the dome of the sky and the Sampo, a device that brings its possessor great fortune and whose precise nature is still debated. The land of Väinölä is set against Pohjola, whose mistress is Louhi, and the poems tell of voyages and quarrels between them and of the making and robbery of the Sampo.

The first version, the Old Kalevala, appeared in 1835 and 1836 with 12,078 verses in thirty-two poems. The standard version, published in 1849, has fifty poems and 22,795 verses. Lönnrot also compiled a lyrical companion collection, the Kanteletar, in 1840.

How much of the text is Lönnrot's own is still argued. He merged variants and characters, left out verses that did not fit and wrote connecting lines. The historian Väinö Kaukonen estimated that about 3 per cent of the lines are Lönnrot's own composition, 14 per cent his compositions from variants, 50 per cent verses kept mostly unchanged and 33 per cent unedited oral poetry.

The Kalevala is regarded as the national epic of Finland and Karelia and was important in forming Finnish national identity and in the language struggle that led to independence from Russia in 1917. It has been translated over 150 times into more than 60 languages. Composers from Filip von Schantz to Jean Sibelius, whose Kullervo dates from 1892, took subjects from it, and Akseli Gallen-Kallela is the painter most associated with it.
kalidasa: Little is known of Kalidasa's life beyond what can be inferred from his poetry and plays. His name means servant of Kali. His works cannot be dated precisely, but they were most likely written during the Gupta era. Several ancient and medieval books say he was a court poet of a king named Vikramaditya. A king of that name is said to have ruled from Ujjain around the 1st century BCE, though some scholars think he is not historical, and other Ujjain kings took the title, notably Chandragupta II (r. 380–415 CE). The most popular theory places Kalidasa in the reign of Chandragupta II.

Scholars have placed his birthplace in Bengal, Kashmir, Vidarbha and Malava. V. V. Mirashi argues for Ujjayini because the poet describes it with such affection; in the Meghaduta the cloud is told not to miss it even if it means a detour. Lachhmi Dhar Kalla argued for Kashmir from the plants, animals and landscape in the works. His name is first mentioned, with that of the poet Bhāravi, in the Aihole inscription of 634 CE in Karnataka.

Most modern scholars attribute seven works to Kalidasa: two epic poems, the Kumārasambhava and the Raghuvaṃśa; two lyric poems, the Meghadūta and the Ṛtusaṃhāra; and three plays, the Abhijñānaśākuntalam, the Mālavikāgnimitram and the Vikramōrvaśīyam. The Kumārasambhava describes the birth and youth of Pārvatī, her marriage to Śiva and the birth of their son Kumāra, and the Raghuvaṃśa tells of the kings of the Raghu dynasty. The Meghadūta describes a Yakṣa sending a message to his lover by a cloud.

In the Abhijñānaśākuntalam, King Duṣyanta meets and marries Śakuntalā; a curse makes him forget her until he sees the ring he gave her, which she has lost. It is generally regarded as a masterpiece and was among the first Sanskrit works translated into English, by Sir William Jones in 1791, after which it was received with wonder by Herder and Goethe. A large number of other works have been wrongly attributed to him.

According to legend Kalidasa was once a simple cowherd who gained learning through the blessing of the goddess Kali. The 7th-century writer Bāṇabhaṭṭa praised his sayings as sweet as honey-laden flowers, and Jayadeva called him the lord of poets. His influence extends to all later Sanskrit works, and the earliest surviving commentaries on his works are those of the Kashmirian scholar Vallabhadeva in the 10th century.
kaliningrad-oblast: Kaliningrad Oblast covers 15,125 square kilometres and is bordered by Poland to the south, Lithuania to the north and east, and the Baltic Sea to the west. It has sea access, so it is described as a semi-exclave. It is mainly flat, with its highest point, Gora Dozor, at 230 metres. The river Pregolya, its largest, drains through the Vistula Lagoon into the Baltic, and the Curonian Lagoon is shared with Lithuania. The port of Baltiysk is Russia's only Baltic port that remains ice-free all year. The oblast also holds amber, and many Russians call it the Amber Land.

The area was inhabited by the Old Prussians and other Western Balts before the Teutonic conquest in the 13th century, after which Germans settled it extensively. The Teutonic Order founded Königsberg in 1255 on the site of a destroyed Sambian settlement called Tvanksta, naming it for Ottokar II of Bohemia. The Lithuanian-inhabited areas of the Teutonic State were known as Lithuania Minor, which covered all of the modern oblast until the 18th century, and the Old Prussians died out through Germanisation in the first half of the 18th century. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg secularised the Order's Prussian branch and made himself ruler of the Duchy of Prussia, the first Protestant state in Europe, with Königsberg as its residence.

Königsberg was a place of Polish and Lithuanian printing, including the first Lithuanian grammar and the first Polish translation of the New Testament, and its Albertina University received a royal privilege from King Sigismund II Augustus in 1560. In 1807, after the defeat at Jena–Auerstedt, the Prussian court fled to Königsberg, and the battles of Eylau and Friedland were followed by the Treaties of Tilsit.

The territory was the northern part of East Prussia and overwhelmingly German. After the defeat of Nazi Germany in the Second World War the Soviet Union annexed it into the Russian SFSR. The flight and expulsion of the Germans left it largely empty until Soviet citizens, mostly ethnic Russians, were settled there. When Lithuania became independent in 1990 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the oblast was cut off from the rest of Russia, and land links now cross neighbouring states. Königsberg Cathedral was restored in the 1990s.

Kaliningrad Oblast is a federal subject of Russia, with its largest city and administrative centre at Kaliningrad, formerly Königsberg. Its population is roughly one million, and Russians form the large majority. Before 1945 the region was overwhelmingly Lutheran.
kalisz: Kalisz lies on the Prosna river in the south-east of Greater Poland, the region regarded as the cradle of the Polish state, and with Poznań is one of its two traditional capitals. Its name is thought to come from the archaic word kal, meaning swamp or marsh. Roman-era finds in the area suggest a stop on the Amber Trail to the Baltic Sea.

Excavations show an early medieval settlement of the Piast period, and the modern town was most likely founded in the 9th century as a castellany and minor fort. In 1106 Bolesław III Wrymouth captured it for his domain. Between 1253 and 1260 it was incorporated under the German town law of Środa Śląska, a variant of Magdeburg law, and during the fragmentation of Poland it formed a separate duchy under a local branch of the Piast dynasty.

The Statute of Kalisz of 1264, issued by Bolesław the Pious, protected Jews at a time of persecution in Western Europe, and in later centuries Poland became a destination for Jewish migration.  In 1314 Ladislaus the Short made it capital of the Kalisz Voivodeship. Casimir III the Great signed a peace treaty with the Order there in 1343.

Kalisz was annexed by Prussia in the Second Partition of 1793, regained by Poles after the Greater Poland uprising of 1806 and, after Napoleon's fall, became a provincial capital of Congress Poland. In August 1914 German forces shelled the city and burned it to the ground, although the Russian troops had left without a fight; of about 68,000 inhabitants only 5,000 remained a year later, and much of the centre was rebuilt by the war's end.

After the German invasion of 1939 the city was annexed by Germany. The Wehrmacht executed Polish defenders in the city and at Winiary, and the Intelligenzaktion targeted the Polish intelligentsia. The Germans set up a Germanisation camp for Polish children taken from their parents. About 30,000 local Jews were murdered by the end of the war, and 20,000 local Catholics were murdered or expelled. The population in 1945 was 43,000, about half the pre-war figure.

Kalisz is the second-largest city of the Greater Poland Voivodeship, with 97,905 residents in December 2021, and is the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kalisz, created in 1992. It is a historical burial site of Piast dukes and medieval Polish monarchs.
kalmar: Kalmar lies in the south-east of Sweden by the Baltic Sea, in the province and cultural region of Småland. It is the seat of Kalmar Municipality and the capital of Kalmar County, and the main route to the island of Öland crosses the Öland Bridge beside it. From the thirteenth to the seventeenth centuries it was one of Sweden's most important cities. The oldest evidence of a town dates from the 11th century. Kalmar's oldest city seal, from between 1255 and 1267, is the oldest known city seal in Scandinavia.

The first foundations of a castle were laid in the 12th century with a round tower for guard and lookout, and the tower was expanded in the 13th century. There Queen Margaret called an assembly of the heads of state of Sweden and Norway, and on 13 July 1397 the Kalmar Union treaty was signed, creating a union that lasted until 1523. At the time the Scanian lands, the provinces of Blekinge, Halland and Scania, belonged to Denmark, so Kalmar's position near the border, together with its harbour and trade, drew it into several feuds.

Two events are independently called the Kalmar Bloodbath: in 1505, when King John had the mayor and city council executed, and in 1599, by order of Duke Charles, later King Charles IX of Sweden. In the 1540s King Gustav Vasa and later his sons Erik XIV and John III rebuilt the castle as the Renaissance castle seen today. Kalmar became a diocese of the Church of Sweden in 1603 and the capital of the newly founded Kalmar County in 1634. The city suffered in the Kalmar War of 1611–1613, which began with a Danish siege of the castle, and counted 22 sieges in all, the last during the Scanian War in the 1670s; the castle was never taken.

After the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658 the borders of Sweden moved further south and Kalmar's strategic importance faded. In 1689 the king set up his main naval base at Karlskrona, and Kalmar lost its place as one of the main military outposts. A new fortified town was built on Kvarnholmen around the mid-1600s on baroque lines. Kalmar Cathedral, designed by Nicodemus Tessin the Elder and begun in 1660, was interrupted several times, including during the Scanian War, and finished in 1703.

Kalmar had 41,388 inhabitants in 2020 and is the third largest urban area in Småland. The city has a university, parts of Linnaeus University, and its cathedral is a leading example of baroque classicism in Sweden.
kalmar-union: The union was the work of Scandinavian aristocrats who wanted to counter the influence of the Hanseatic League, a northern German trade league centred on the Baltic and North Seas. Denmark had recently suffered a humiliating defeat in the Danish-Hanseatic War of 1361 to 1370. On the personal level it was achieved by Queen Margaret I of Denmark, daughter of King Valdemar IV of Denmark and wife of King Haakon VI of Norway and Sweden. Her son Olaf inherited the Danish crown in 1376 and the Norwegian crown in 1380.

When Olaf died in 1387 Margaret became regent of Denmark and Norway and adopted her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania. After she defeated King Albert in 1389, with the help Swedish nobles had asked of her, Eric was proclaimed King of Norway and was elected King of Denmark and Sweden in 1396. The union joined under one monarch the three kingdoms and Norway's maritime possessions, which included Iceland, Greenland, the Faroe Islands, Orkney and Shetland.

The union was never continuous. The Engelbrekt rebellion, which began in 1434, led to the overthrow of King Eric in Denmark and Sweden in 1439 and in Norway in 1442. The three kingdoms had been united without a break for a long time until the death of Christopher of Bavaria in 1448. Christian of Oldenburg then became king of Denmark, and of Norway from 1450, and Karl Knutsson Bonde ruled in Sweden. After Karl's death, Christian was defeated by Sten Sture the Elder at the Battle of Brunkeberg in 1471, and Sweden was mostly governed by protectors of the realm.

In 1520 Christian II invaded Sweden, killed Sten Sture the Younger at the Battle of Bogesund and was crowned king, and supporters of Sture were executed in the Stockholm Bloodbath. Gustav Vasa, whose father was among those executed, raised a rebellion in Dalarna and allied with Lübeck. His election as King of Sweden on 6 June 1523 ended the union for Sweden, and Frederick I renounced his claim in 1524 at the Treaty of Malmö.

A remnant lasted until 1536 or 1537, when the Danish Privy Council declared Norway a Danish province, though it kept its own laws. The union of Denmark and Norway lasted nearly three centuries, until Norway was ceded to Sweden in 1814. The historian Sverre Bagge explains the union's instability by the power of the national aristocracies, the different effects of its foreign policy on each kingdom, and the difficulty of controlling so large a territory.
kalmyks: The Kalmyks are the only Mongolic people in Europe. They are a branch of the Oirat Mongols, whose grazing-lands spanned parts of present-day Kazakhstan, Russia, Mongolia and China. After the fall of the Yuan dynasty in 1368 the Oirats struggled for 400 years against the Khalkha Mongols, the Ming and the Qing for control of Mongolia; the struggle ended in 1757 with the defeat of the Dzungar Khanate by the Qing. The Kalmyks descend chiefly from the Torghut, with smaller groups of Dörbets, Khoshuts and Dzungars. The name is of Turkic origin and means remnant or to remain.

In the early 17th century the First Altan Khan drove the Oirats west to eastern Kazakhstan, where the Torghuts were blocked by the Kazakhs from trading with towns on the Syr Darya and turned to the new Russian outposts. In 1618 the Torghuts and a contingent of Dörbets, 200,000 to 250,000 people under their taishi Kho Orluk, chose to migrate to the lower Volga. They reached the region in 1630 and encamped on land that had belonged to the Astrakhan Khanate and was claimed by Russia. The Kalmyks became Russian allies, and a treaty to protect the southern Russian border was signed with the Kalmyk Khanate. The Oirats expelled most of the Nogai Horde and made the remaining nomadic tribes their vassals.

After the exodus of 1771 the Kalmyks who stayed in the Russian Empire continued their nomadic life between the Don and the Volga. The Soviet government set up the Kalmyk Autonomous Oblast in November 1920, with Elista as its capital, and in October 1935 it became an autonomous republic. On 28 December 1943 the Soviet government accused them of collaborating with the Germans and deported the entire population to Central Asia and Siberia within 24 hours, at night in winter, in unheated cattle cars. In 1957 Khrushchev permitted the Kalmyks to return, and Kalmykia again became an autonomous republic in 1958.

The Kalmyks embraced Tibetan Buddhism in the early 17th century and belong to the Gelug school, the Yellow Hat sect. Their clergy trained either in monasteries on the steppe, many of which were felt tents that moved with the tribes, or in Tibet. In the 17th century the Khoshut monk Zaya Pandita devised Clear Script, based on the vertical Mongol script, to write Oirat. They live mainly in the Republic of Kalmykia between the Volga and the Don, and small communities live in the United States, France, Germany and the Czech Republic.
kama-river: The Kama, also known as the Chulman in Tatar, is 1,805 kilometres long and drains a basin of 507,000 square kilometres. It is the longest left tributary of the Volga and the largest by discharge. It starts near Kuliga in the Udmurt Republic, flows northwest for 200 kilometres, turns northeast near Loyno for another 200 kilometres, then turns south and west through Perm Krai, again through the Udmurt Republic and through Tatarstan, where it meets the Volga south of Kazan. Its largest tributaries include the Vishera, the Chusovaya, the Belaya and the Vyatka.

Before the advent of railroads, important portages connected the Kama with the basins of the Northern Dvina and the Pechora. In the early nineteenth century the Northern Ekaterininsky Canal linked the upper Kama with the Vychegda River, a tributary of the Northern Dvina, but it was mostly abandoned after just a few years because of low use.

The Kama is dammed at Perm by the Kama Hydroelectric Station, at Chaykovsky by the Votkinsk Hydroelectric Station and at Naberezhnye Chelny by the Nizhnekamsk Hydroelectric Station, each forming a reservoir. The reservoirs have significantly altered the native fish communities and allowed alien species to spread: invasive fish make up 8 per cent of the species in the upper reservoirs and 27 per cent in the Votkinsk Reservoir.

Which river is the tributary has long been disputed. At the confluence the Kama carries 4,100 cubic metres a second against the Volga's 3,500, its source lies at 331 metres against the Volga's 228, and its valley is held to be more ancient. The Volga, however, has the larger basin, 604,000 square kilometres against the Kama's 507,000.
kamakura: Kamakura is surrounded to the north, east and west by hills and to the south by the open water of Sagami Bay, which made it a natural fortress. Before tunnels and modern roads linked it to Fujisawa, Ōfuna and Zushi, it could be entered by land only through narrow artificial passes. The seven most important were called Kamakura's Seven Entrances. The name of the city is explained by the most likely theory as a comparison of this enclosed shape with a cooking hearth (kamado) and a warehouse (kura), both of which are open on one side only.

Traces of settlement in the area go back at least 10,000 years. In the Jōmon period the sea stood higher than now, and the flat land up to Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū lay under water, so the oldest pottery comes from hillside settlements dated between 7500 and 5000 BCE. The name appears in the Kojiki of 712, but the city enters the historical record clearly only with the founding of the Kamakura shogunate by Minamoto no Yoritomo. After his family had been almost wiped out by the Taira clan, he became the most powerful man in the land and set up the first military government in Japan, an institution that lasted 141 years.

The fall of the shogunate began the Muromachi period, an age of disorder. Kamakura declined slowly and, as capital of the Kantō region, dominated the east of the country for almost as long as the shogunate had lasted. In 1335 Hōjō Tokiyuki, son of the last regent Takatoki, tried to restore the shogunate by force and defeated Ashikaga Tadayoshi, Kamakura's de facto ruler. Ashikaga Takauji came from Kyoto to help his brother and defeated Tokiyuki at Koshigoe. Kamakura came out of this period almost completely destroyed. In the Edo period it became a popular destination for the townspeople of Edo, and after the Meiji Restoration its temples, beach and reputation made it popular again.

Kamakura is a city in Kanagawa Prefecture, designated as a city on 3 November 1939, with an estimated 172,929 inhabitants in 2020. Its monumental bronze statue of Amida Buddha at Kōtoku-in has stood outdoors since a 15th-century tsunami destroyed the temple that housed it. The city also has the Five Great Zen Temples and thousands of yagura, caves dug into the hillsides in the Middle Ages as tombs for high-ranking people and priests. The Great Kantō earthquake of 1923 devastated much of the city, and damaged temples and shrines have since been restored.
kamianets-podilskyi: Kamianets-Podilskyi stands on the Smotrych River, 18 km from its confluence with the Dniester, in the Podolian Upland, whose elevated ridges known as Tovtry give the area a canyon-like relief. It is a historical centre of the Podillia region and served as capital of the Duchy of Podolia, the Podolian Voivodeship, the Podolia Eyalet, the Podolia Governorate and the Podolian District. The name means the Stone of Podilia, from the Old Slavic kamen, stone, and the region's name. Some historians hold that the ancient Dacians founded a settlement on the spot called Petridava or Klepidava.

The city is first mentioned in 1062, when it belonged to the principality of Terebovlia, and later to Halych and the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia. About 1230 Prince Lev Danilovich invited Armenians to defend the eastern border and rewarded them with estates near the town. Mongol invaders destroyed it in 1241. Casimir III of Poland inherited it in 1352, and in 1374 Prince George Koriatovich granted it Magdeburg Law. It became the seat of a Latin Catholic diocese in 1378 and in 1434 the capital of the Podolian Voivodeship. Polish kings expanded the castle to defend Poland against Ottoman and Tatar invasions, so that it was called the gateway to Poland. Separate Ruthenian and Armenian courts worked in the city from the late 15th century.

The Ottomans and their ally the hetman Petro Doroshenko captured the city in 1672, and it became the capital of the Podolia Eyalet. The Ottomans expelled the Armenians in 1674. The population fell almost tenfold under Ottoman rule, which ended in 1699 when the Treaty of Karlowitz returned the city to Poland under Augustus II the Strong. In November 1757 Bishop Dembowski, at the instigation of the Frankists, ordered copies of the Talmud found in his bishopric confiscated and burned; accounts differ over whether up to a thousand copies or only one were destroyed.

After the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 the city belonged to the Russian Empire and was the capital of the Podolia Governorate. The fortifications were disbanded in 1808 and the fortress became a prison. The city was occupied by Austria-Hungary in 1915 and was the temporary capital of the Ukrainian People's Republic in 1919 to 1920. After the Ukrainian-Soviet War it formed part of Soviet Ukraine, and Kamianets-Podilskyi has been part of independent Ukraine since 24 August 1991.

The city had 96,896 inhabitants by a 2022 estimate. Poles, Jews and Ukrainians have dominated its population, with a substantial Armenian minority, and the city still has Polish, Ruthenian and Armenian market squares. Its landmarks include the castle, the Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul, the 14th-century Ruthenian Gate and the 15th-century Saint Nicholas Armenian Church.
kampala: Kampala is a hilly place whose valleys are filled with sluggish rivers, lakes and swamps. The city proper covers 189 square kilometres, of which 13 are water. Its highest point is the summit of Kololo hill at 1,311 metres, in the centre of the city, and its lowest is the shore of Lake Victoria to the south at 1,135 metres. It lies on the East African Plateau between the two arms of the East African Rift and has a tropical rainforest climate with two wetter seasons.

The area of hills and swamps that became Kampala was part of the core of the highly centralised Kingdom of Buganda. Each Kabaka, on coronation or later in his reign, could set up his capital, the Kibuga, on a new hill, so the royal capital shifted. The first written description of the Kibuga was by the explorer Richard Burton in The Lake Region of East Africa, published in 1860, drawing on the information of an Arab trader. He described a settlement a day's journey long, with a palace at least a mile long and circular huts in a line, surrounded by a strong fence with four gates.

The name Kampala at first referred only to Old Kampala hill, where Fort Lugard stood. The hill had been a hunting reserve of the Kabaka, with several kinds of antelope, especially the impala, and the British officials who were allotted it called it the Hill of the Impala. In 1900 the regents of the infant Kabaka Daudi Cwa II signed the Buganda Agreement with Sir Harry Johnston for the British government. It created new forms of land tenure, among them freehold, Crown land and mailo, and divided the land in a way that came to shape the development of Kampala.

Kampala is the capital and largest city of Uganda, with a city proper of nearly two million people and a metropolitan area that includes the neighbouring districts of Wakiso, Mukono, Mpigi, Buikwe and Luweero. The city is the seat of the Buganda kingdom at Mengo. The Kasubi Tombs, burial ground of the Buganda kings, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Uganda Museum and the National Theatre are among its cultural institutions. A Bahá'í House of Worship, the Mother Temple of Africa, stands on Kikaya Hill on its outskirts.
kana: Old Japanese was written entirely in Chinese characters, and a set of them called man'yōgana was first used to represent the sounds of grammatical particles and morphemes. There was no consistent method, so one sound could be written with many characters; the Man'yōshū, an anthology assembled sometime after 759, uses as many as almost twenty for the mora ka. Hiragana developed from cursive man'yōgana, and katakana from abbreviated parts of regular-script man'yōgana, first as a system of glosses adding readings or explanations to Buddhist sutras. The shapes of many hiragana resemble Chinese cursive script, and those of many katakana the Korean gugyeol.

Kana is traditionally said to have been invented by the Buddhist priest Kūkai in the ninth century. He certainly brought the Siddhaṃ script of India home from China in 806, and his interest in the sacred aspects of speech led him to conclude that Japanese would be better written phonetically.

Each kana corresponds to one syllable or phoneme. Apart from the five vowels it is always a consonant followed by a vowel, with the single exception of the sign for the nasal n, which is usually romanised n. The limited number of Japanese phonemes and the rigid syllable structure make kana an accurate representation of the spoken language. Voiced consonants are written with the voicing mark dakuten, and p sounds with the half-voicing mark handakuten.

The name is a compound of kari, meaning borrowed, and na, name, and was used in contrast to mana, true name, the kanji used for their meaning. Hiragana was historically called women's script because it was used by women, while men, who were more educated, wrote phonetic kanji, called otokogana. Until the 18th century the script was seen from a Sinocentric view; the kokugaku movement then began to treat it as a national writing system distinct from Chinese characters.

Hiragana and katakana did not quickly supplant man'yōgana. The present set was codified only in 1900, and the older variants are called hentaigana. The spelling reforms of 1946 abolished the kana for wi, we and wo, keeping wo only as the accusative particle. Hiragana is the default script for native words, particles and inflections, while katakana is used for words of foreign origin, foreign names, onomatopoeia, emphasis and technical terms. Small kana written beside rarer kanji to show their pronunciation are called furigana, and are used widely in children's books.
kanazawa: Kanazawa lies in north-western Ishikawa Prefecture in the Hokuriku region, bordered by the Sea of Japan to the west and Toyama Prefecture to the east, between the Sai and Asano rivers. Its name means marsh of gold and is said to come from the legend of the peasant Imohori Togoro, who was digging potatoes when flakes of gold washed up. The area was originally known as Ishiura and was part of ancient Kaga Province.

During the Muromachi period Kaga Province came under the Ikkō-ikki, followers of the Jōdo Shinshū priest Rennyo, who displaced the Togashi clan and set up a theocratic republic later called the Peasants' Kingdom. Their stronghold, the Kanazawa Gobo, stood on the tip of the Kodatsuno Ridge, a natural fortress around which a castle town developed. In 1580 Oda Nobunaga sent Shibata Katsuie and his general Sakuma Morimasa to conquer the Ikkō-ikki. After Nobunaga's assassination in 1582 Maeda Toshiie displaced Morimasa and founded Kaga Domain. At Sekigahara in 1600 Maeda sided with Tokugawa Ieyasu and enlarged his holdings to 1.2 million koku, by far the largest domain under the shogunate. The Maeda ruled from Kanazawa Castle to the end of the Edo period.

The Maeda enlarged the castle and planned the surrounding castle town for defence. Before the Maeda the town had a population of only 5,000; by 1700 it exceeded 100,000, rivalling Rome, Amsterdam and Madrid, and reached about 120,000 in 1710. All samurai of Kaga, whatever their income, lived in Kanazawa, and by the late 17th century over three-quarters of the town was samurai housing.

The Maeda directed their wealth into arts and crafts rather than military pursuits, which helped ease the shogunate's suspicion of this Tozama daimyō. Toshitsune formed the Kaga Workmanship Office and promoted lacquer and gold-and-lacquer-work, and Maeda Tsunanori collected art and artisans from across the country. After the Meiji Restoration the modern city was created on 1 April 1889, with an area of 10.40 square kilometres that grew by annexation to 468.64.

Kanazawa is the capital of Ishikawa Prefecture, with an estimated 466,029 people in 2018. The Higashi Chaya District keeps geisha houses of the Edo period with plain two-storey wooden façades, and merchant houses were long and thin because houses were taxed on frontage width. Gold leaf is central to its crafts: Kanazawa produces 99% of Japan's high-quality gold leaf, which covered the Golden Pavilion in Kyoto, and its lacquerware is traditionally decorated with gold dust. The cultural landscape of its castle town has been designated an Important Cultural Landscape.
kangxi-emperor: The Kangxi Emperor was born on 4 May 1654 in the Forbidden City, Beijing, the third son of the Shunzhi Emperor, and was given the personal name Xuanye. He was enthroned on 7 February 1661 at the age of seven, though his era name Kangxi was first used on 18 February 1662. Four regents appointed by his father held actual power: Sonin, Suksaha, Ebilun and Oboi. After Sonin died, Oboi put Suksaha to death and became sole regent, an arrangement the young emperor and the court accepted for some years.

In 1673 three Ming generals who had aided the Qing, Wu Sangui, Geng Jingzhong and Shang Zhixin, controlled large fiefs in the south and west. Against the advice of most of his advisers, Kangxi tried to make them give up their lands, and the result was a rebellion lasting eight years. He relied mainly on Han Chinese Green Standard Army soldiers, granted clemency to common people caught up in the war, and won in 1681. In later years he blamed himself in part for the loss of life.

In 1683 Qing ships under Admiral Shi Lang defeated the Ming loyalist forces of the Kingdom of Tungning off Penghu, and Zheng Keshuang surrendered Taiwan. Border conflicts with the Tsardom of Russia on the Amur ended with the Treaty of Nerchinsk in 1689, which set a border between Russia and China. Against the Dzungar Khanate the emperor campaigned in person. In 1720 a larger expedition took Lhasa from the Dzungars, who had held it for three years.

At court Kangxi ordered the compilation of the Kangxi Dictionary, the Complete Tang Poems and the Complete Classics Collection of Ancient China, and persuaded scholars still loyal to the Ming to work on the dictionary without formally serving the Qing. He welcomed Jesuits such as Ferdinand Verbiest, who ran the imperial observatory, and in 1692 issued an Edict of Toleration for Catholicism. That tolerance ended with the Chinese Rites controversy.

The succession was disputed for years. His son Yinreng was named crown prince at the age of two, but was later deposed, and the princes quarrelled over the throne in what is known as the Nine Lords' War. Kangxi died on 20 December 1722 at the age of 68. According to official records he had summoned seven sons to his bedside, and the fourth prince, Yinzhen, became the Yongzheng Emperor. His reign of 61 years is the longest of any Chinese emperor, and began the High Qing era.
kannada: Kannada, like Malayalam and Tamil, is a South Dravidian language and a descendant of Tamil-Kannada, from which it derives its grammar and core vocabulary. Its history is divided into Old Kannada, from 450 to 1200, Middle Kannada from 1200 to 1700, and Modern Kannada from 1700. It has been influenced by Sanskrit and Prakrit and has many Sanskrit loan words.

The earliest Kannada inscriptions date from the middle of the 5th century. The Halmidi inscription, usually dated to about 450, is the earliest well-attested full-length stone inscription in Kannada, and its existence indicates that the language had become an administrative one by then.

Kannada is spoken mainly in Karnataka in south-western India, where it is the official and administrative language, and by minorities in neighbouring states. It had 43.7 million native speakers in India at the 2011 census, and it has been declared a Classical language of India. It is written in the Kannada script, which evolved from the 5th-century Kadamba script. The script is syllabic and almost entirely phonetic, with forty-nine letters. The canonical word order is subject–object–verb.

Kannada was the court language of many dynasties of South India and the Deccan, including the Kadambas, the Western Ganga dynasty, the Rashtrakutas, the Hoysalas and the Vijayanagara Empire. The oldest known literary work is the Kavirājamārga, a work on poetics linked to the Rashtrakuta king Nṛpatuṅga Amoghavarṣa I in about 850. Pampa, regarded as the first poet of Kannada, was one of the three gems of Jaina literature along with Ponna and Ranna.

The vacana tradition of Śaiva devotional writing, with Basavanna, Allama Prabhu and Akka Mahadevi, emerged around the turn of the second millennium in the common language. Between the 13th and 18th centuries literature turned to devotional themes, and the Haridāsas, among them Kanakadāsa and Purandaradāsa, spread bhakti literature through music. Kannada literature has received eight Jnanpith Awards, the most of any Indian language.
kano-state: Kano State is in the north of Nigeria. It was created on 27 May 1967 from the former Northern Region and borders Katsina State on the north-west, Jigawa State on the north-east, Bauchi State on the south-east and Kaduna State on the south-west. A part of it became Jigawa State in 1991. The state capital is Kano. The Hausa and Fulani make up most of the population, Hausa is the dominant language, and Hausa and Fulfulde are the official languages. The state observes Sharia law within the framework of the Nigerian constitution. It has 44 local government areas.

The area was the site of several kingdoms and empires. The Kingdom of Kano was centred on Dalla Hill from about 1000 to 1349. In 1349 the Sultanate of Kano was established when Yaji I converted to Islam and became its first sultan. Kurmi Market opened in 1463 and helped the city of Kano become a centre of commercial activity in Hausaland. It is still open, and its importance is reflected in the state's nickname, Centre of Commerce. In the 16th and 17th centuries the sultanate became one of the most powerful Hausa kingdoms.

After the Fulani jihad of 1804 to 1808 the Kano Emirate replaced the sultanate. Emir Ibrahim Dabo made administrative reforms to increase commerce, and leaders encouraged traders to move from Katsina, taking advantage of raids from the Hausa Sultanate of Maradi. The British Empire conquered the Kano Emirate in 1903 and incorporated it into the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. The main ethnic groups in pre-colonial Kano were the Hausa, Fulani, Barebari (Kanuri), Tuareg, Arabs and Nupe.

Kano has many large markets, including Kurmi, Kantin Kwari, Sabon Gari and Dawanau, and many specialise in products such as textiles or grain. The dye industry has contributed to the economy since the 19th century. During the colonial period and for several years after independence, the groundnuts grown in the state were one of the country's major sources of revenue. Millet, cowpeas, sorghum, maize and rice are grown for local use, and groundnuts and cotton for export and industry. Industries include textiles, tanning, footwear, plastics and pharmaceuticals. Attractions include Kurmi Market, Kano's city wall, Gidan Rumfa, the emir's palace, the Kano Museum and Dalla Hill.
kansas: Kansas is a landlocked state on the Great Plains, bordered by Nebraska to the north, Colorado to the west, Oklahoma to the south and Missouri to the east. It is generally considered the geographic centre of the contiguous United States, with Lebanon in Smith County approximately the centre. Its highest point is Mount Sunflower, at 1,231 m. The name comes from the Kansas River, named after the Kansa or Kaw people, and ultimately from the Algonquian term Akansa, which referred to the Quapaw.

Before European colonisation the area was occupied by the Caddoan Wichita and later the Siouan Kaw. In the east, people generally lived in villages along the river valleys, while those in the west were semi-nomadic and hunted large herds of bison. The first European to enter present-day Kansas was the Spanish conquistador Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, who explored the area in 1541. Between 1763 and 1803 the territory was part of Spanish Louisiana. Most of modern Kansas was acquired by the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, and the south-west was ceded after the Mexican–American War in 1848.

From 1812 to 1821 Kansas was part of the Missouri Territory. The Santa Fe Trail crossed it from 1821 to 1880, carrying manufactured goods from Missouri and silver and furs from Santa Fe, and wagon ruts from the trail are still visible in the prairie. The first settlement of non-Indigenous people took place in 1827 at Fort Leavenworth, and settlement quickened in the 1850s during the political wars over slavery.

The Kansas–Nebraska Act officially opened Kansas to settlement in 1854. Conflict then broke out between abolitionist Free-Staters from New England and pro-slavery settlers from neighbouring Missouri over whether it would be a free or a slave state, a period known as Bleeding Kansas. Kansas entered the Union as a free state on 29 January 1861, whence the unofficial nickname The Free State. The Homestead Acts of 1862 brought further settlers, and the cattle trade of the 1870s drew some of the best-known figures of the Wild West to the west of the state. From 1887 Kansas women could vote in city elections and hold certain offices.

Topeka is the capital and Wichita the most populous city, while the largest urban area is the Kansas City metropolitan area, which straddles the border with Missouri. The 2020 census counted 2,937,880 people. Nearly 90 per cent of the land is devoted to agriculture, with wheat, corn, sorghum and soybeans among the main crops, and the state also has a large aerospace industry. Kansas is the setting of Dorothy Gale's home in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900), and its state anthem is Home on the Range, written by Brewster Higley.
kapan: Kapan lies in the narrow valley of the Voghji River on the southeastern slopes of the Zangezur Mountains, between the Bargushat and Meghri ridges, on the northern slopes of Mount Khustup, which at 3,201 metres is the highest peak of the region. Its elevation is 750 to 1,050 metres. The name comes from the Classical Armenian kapan, meaning mountain pass. It later became Ghap'an, which was in use until 1991, when the older form was restored.

The area was first mentioned in the 5th century as a small settlement among the properties of the Siunia dynasty, in the Baghk' canton of Syunik, the ninth province of historic Greater Armenia. Prince Dzagik fortified it in the late 9th and early 10th century, and it became the residence of the Dzagikian princes. By the end of the 10th century Prince Smbat II moved to Kapan and founded the Kingdom of Syunik, proclaiming himself king under the protectorate of the Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia. As its capital Kapan flourished in the 11th century, reaching around 20 thousand inhabitants, mostly Armenians with a prominent Jewish minority, and was a centre of trade, crafts and metallurgy.

In 1103 Seljuk invaders ruined it; the historian Stephen Orbelian says they began their massacres in the Jewish quarter. After the kingdom fell in 1170 Syunik suffered Seljuk, Mongol, Aq Qoyunlu and Kara Koyunlu invasions between the 12th and 15th centuries.

In the early 16th century Kapan became part of the Erivan Province of Safavid Iran. In 1722 the noble families of Syunik united in an Armenian principality of Kapan, and the military leader David Bek began the campaign against the Iranians and the invading Ottoman Turks, helped by thousands of local Armenians including Avan Yuzbashi and Mkhitar Sparapet. The centre of his struggle was the Baghaberd Fortress northwest of Kapan and the Halidzor Fortress, where he died in 1728.

In 1813 Syunik became part of the Russian Empire under the Treaty of Gulistan. In the first half of the 19th century Russian and German engineers and workers came to work in the region's copper mines, and Greek specialists arrived in 1850.

Kapan is a town in southeastern Armenia and the capital of Syunik Province, which was formed in 1995 after Armenia's independence. The town received city status in 1938 and was a major mining and industrial centre of Soviet Armenia, known as Kafan in Russian. It is almost entirely Armenian and its population was 43,190 in 2011. Heritage monuments in the area include the Baghaberd Fortress and a medieval bridge dating from 871.
karachay-cherkessia: Karachay-Cherkessia lies on the slopes of the north-western Caucasus, stretching 140 kilometres from north to south and 170 kilometres from east to west, and mountains cover 80 per cent of its territory. Mount Elbrus, at 5,642 metres the highest peak in the Caucasus, stands on its border with Kabardino-Balkaria. The republic borders Krasnodar Krai, Stavropol Krai, Kabardino-Balkaria and Georgia. A total of 172 rivers flow through it, the largest being the Kuban, the Bolshoy Zelenchuk, the Maly Zelenchuk, the Urup and the Laba, and it has about 130 glacial mountain lakes.

The Karachay-Cherkess Autonomous Oblast was founded on 12 January 1922, in the early years of the Soviet Union. On 26 April 1926 it was divided into the Karachay Autonomous Oblast and the Cherkess National Okrug, which became an autonomous oblast in 1928. In November 1943 the Karachay Autonomous Oblast was abolished; the Karachay were accused of collaboration with the Nazis and 70,000 of them were deported to the Kazakh and Uzbek republics. Most of their territory was divided between Stavropol Krai and the Georgian SSR, and the remaining area, populated by the Cherkess, remained the Cherkess Autonomous Oblast.

On 9 January 1957, after the rehabilitation of the Karachay, the Cherkess oblast was merged with the restored Karachay territory in the former borders of the Karachay-Cherkess Autonomous Oblast. It became an Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic on 3 July 1991. In January 1992 Boris Yeltsin was prepared to accept its division, and a commission on forming three autonomous regions, Karachay, Cherkess and Batalpashinsk, was set up. According to official results a referendum on 28 March 1992 produced a majority against splitting, and on 9 December 1992 the republic was recognised as the Karachay-Cherkess Republic.

The Karachay-Cherkess Republic is one of Russia's ethnic republics, in the North Caucasian Federal District, with its capital at Cherkessk. The Karachays, a Caucasian Turkic people, form the largest group, followed by Russians, Cherkess and Abazins. It has five official languages: Russian, Abaza, Cherkess (Kabardian), Karachay-Balkar and Nogai. At the Special Astrophysical Observatory on the Zelenchuk River stands the BTA-6 telescope, the largest in the world from 1975 until 1993, and the large radio telescope RATAN-600.
karachi: Karachi lies on the coastline of Sindh province in southern Pakistan, along the Karachi Harbour, a natural harbour on the Arabian Sea. It is built on a coastal plain with scattered rocky outcroppings, hills and marshlands, and mangrove forests grow in the brackish waters around the harbour and farther south-east towards the Indus River Delta. West of the city is Cape Monze, known locally as Ras Muari, an area of sea cliffs, sandstone promontories and beaches. Two small ranges, the Khasa Hills and the Mulri Hills, lie within the city in the north-west. They are barren, part of the larger Kirthar Range, and reach a maximum height of 528 metres.

The region has been inhabited for millennia. Upper Paleolithic and Mesolithic sites have been excavated in the Mulri Hills on the northern outskirts, and their earliest inhabitants are believed to have been hunter-gatherers who left ancient flint tools. The region is believed to have been known to the ancient Greeks and may have been the site of Barbarikon, an ancient seaport at the nearby mouth of the Indus.
