Karachi may also be the place called Ramya in ancient Greek texts.

The modern city was reputedly founded in 1729 as the fortified village of Kolachi-jo-Goth during the rule of the Kalhora dynasty, said to be named in honour of Mai Kolachi, whose son slew a man-eating crocodile. The shortened name Karachee was first used in a Dutch report of 1742 about a shipwreck near the settlement. The village greatly increased in importance with the arrival of the East India Company in the mid-19th century, following the annexation of Sindh. The colonial administration began substantial projects to turn it into a major seaport and to connect it to the railway network of South Asia.

At independence in 1947 Karachi was the largest city in Sindh, with an estimated 400,000 people and a slim Hindu majority. After the partition of British India, hundreds of thousands of Muslim refugees arrived from India while nearly all its Hindu residents left. Karachi served as the federal capital of Pakistan from 1947 to 1959 and grew rapidly, attracting migrants from across the country and other parts of South Asia.

Karachi is the capital of Sindh and the largest city in Pakistan, with about 20 million people according to the census of 2023. It contains the country's two largest seaports, the Port of Karachi and Port Qasim, and its busiest airport, Jinnah International Airport. It is one of the most linguistically, ethnically and religiously diverse cities in Pakistan. Among its landmarks are Frere Hall, Empress Market and St. Patrick's Cathedral, which brought the first neo-Gothic buildings to the city, and Wazir Mansion, the birthplace of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, now a museum.
karaman: Karaman lies in Central Anatolia, north of the Taurus Mountains and about 100 km south of Konya, at an average elevation of 1,039 metres. It has a cold semi-arid climate with hot, dry summers, cold, snowy winters and almost 3,000 hours of sunshine a year. The city takes its name from Karaman Bey, one of the rulers of the Karamanid dynasty. Its earlier name, Laranda, comes from the Luwian Larawanda, meaning a sandy place, and in Hittite times it was known as Lānda.

Little is known of the early history of Laranda. It is first named in the writings of Diodorus Siculus, who says that Perdiccas and King Philip, after defeating Ariarathes I of Cappadocia, set out to punish Laranda and Isauria for killing Balacrus, the general whom Alexander the Great had appointed satrap of the region. Laranda was destroyed, later became a seat of Isaurian pirates and for a time was controlled by Antipater of Derbe, until Amyntas of Galatia killed him. In the early third century CE it was the seat of a bishop, Neon, who approved the preaching of the layman Euelpis there. It belonged to the Roman and then the Byzantine Empire until the Seljuks captured it in the early 12th century.

Frederick Barbarossa occupied the city in 1190 and the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia held it from 1211 to 1216. Karaman Bey took it in 1256 and gave it his name, and from 1275 it was the capital of the Karamanid beylik. The Sufi preacher Bahaeddin Veled arrived in 1222 with his family, and the emir had a madrasah built for them. His son Rumi married his wife Gevher Hatun in Karaman, and Rumi's mother died there in 1224. The Ottoman Empire conquered the Karamanids in 1468 and moved the capital of the province to Konya in 1483.

Karaman is the seat of Karaman Province and had 175,390 inhabitants in 2022. From the Karamanid period it keeps the ruins of a castle and some walls, two mosques and a madrasah. The Aktekke Mosque, also called the Mader-i Mevlana Cami, built in 1370 to replace the original madrasah, holds the graves of Rumi's mother and other family members. The poet Yunus Emre, who lived about 1238 to 1320, spent his later years in Karaman and is believed to lie buried beside the Yunus Emre Mosque.
karelia: Karelia stretches from the White Sea coast to the Gulf of Finland and contains the two largest lakes in Europe, Lake Ladoga and Lake Onega. The Karelian Isthmus lies between the Gulf of Finland and Lake Ladoga. The River Svir is usually thought of as its traditional southern border, and the River Kymi as the historic western border, which separated the Karelians from the Häme Finns in the Middle Ages.

During the Early Middle Ages settlers from western Finland mixed with the local population to form the Karelian ethnic group. Sweden and the Novgorod Republic fought bitterly over Karelia from the 13th century. The Treaty of Nöteborg of 1323 divided it: Sweden received the southern Karelian Isthmus and most of South Karelia, with Viborg as the capital of its province, while Novgorod held the northern isthmus and North and Ladoga Karelia.

By the Treaty of Stolbovo of 1617 large parts of Russian Karelia were ceded to Sweden, and conflict between the new Swedish rulers and the local people led thousands of Karelians to emigrate to Russia. The Treaty of Nystad of 1721 ceded a portion of Karelia to Russia, and the Treaty of Åbo of 1743 ceded South Karelia. After Russia occupied Finland in the Finnish War, these provinces, Old Finland, were incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Finland in 1812. Finland declared independence in 1917, and the Treaty of Tartu of 1920 confirmed the border. The Russian part became a Karelian autonomous republic of the Soviet Union in 1923.

The Winter War of 1939 ended with the Moscow Peace Treaty of March 1940, which handed a large part of Finnish Karelia to the Soviet Union and forced over 400,000 people to relocate within Finland. Finland retook the territory in the Continuation War of 1941 to 1944, occupied much of East Karelia, and was forced out in 1944. It lost its fourth biggest city, Viipuri, its industrial heartland along the River Vuoksi, and access to the fishing waters of Lake Ladoga. One eighth of Finland's citizens became refugees. About one million people in Finland can trace their roots to that area.

Karelia is divided between north-western Russia, in the Republic of Karelia and Leningrad Oblast, and Finland, in the regions of South Karelia, North Karelia and the eastern part of Kymenlaakso. The Republic of Karelia was formed in 1991 from the Karelian autonomous republic. Its capital is Petrozavodsk.
karl-i: Charles was born on 17 August 1887 at the Castle of Persenbeug in Lower Austria, the son of Archduke Otto Franz and Princess Maria Josepha of Saxony. He was raised a devout Catholic and, unusually for the imperial family, attended a public gymnasium, the Schottengymnasium, before entering the army. From 1906 to 1908 he served as an officer chiefly in Prague, where he studied law and political science. On 21 October 1911 he married Princess Zita of Bourbon-Parma. He became heir presumptive in 1914 when his uncle Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated at Sarajevo, an event that precipitated the First World War.

Charles succeeded his grand-uncle Franz Joseph on 21 November 1916, took the title of Supreme Commander of the army on 2 December and was crowned King of Hungary on 30 December. In 1917 he secretly began peace negotiations with France through his brother-in-law Prince Sixtus of Bourbon-Parma, but the Allies insisted that Austria recognise Italian territorial claims and he refused. When the Sixtus Affair leaked in April 1918, Charles denied involvement until French Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau published letters signed by him. Foreign minister Count Czernin resigned, and Austria-Hungary had to give Berlin full control of its armed forces, factories and railways.

From the start Charles favoured a third, Croatian, political entity beside Austria and Hungary, but the Hungarian Parliament vetoed the proposals. On 14 October 1918 he issued a People's Manifesto, and on 29 October the Croatian Sabor ended all ties with Hungary and Austria. On 11 November 1918 he issued a proclamation recognising the Austrian people's right to determine the form of the state and relinquishing every participation in the administration, although the word abdication was never used. He wrote privately that he had not abdicated and never would. In April 1919 the National Assembly dethroned the Habsburgs and banished him from German-Austria for life.

Charles went into exile in Switzerland and in 1921 made two attempts to reclaim the Hungarian throne, which failed largely because the regent, Admiral Miklós Horthy, refused his support. He was arrested and, on 19 November 1921, arrived at his last place of exile, the Portuguese island of Madeira, where he died of respiratory failure on 1 April 1922. Historians have been mixed in their judgements. Helmut Rumpler called him far too weak for the challenges facing him, while others see a brave and honourable man who tried to stop the war. The Catholic Church beatified him in 2004.
karl-marx: Karl Marx was born on 5 May 1818 to Heinrich Marx and Henriette Pressburg at Brückengasse 664 in Trier, then part of the Kingdom of Prussia. His family was originally Jewish but had converted to Christianity before his birth. His father, a lawyer, had converted to the state Evangelical Church of Prussia to keep his career after Prussia annexed the Rhineland and Jewish emancipation was abrogated. Heinrich was a man of the Enlightenment and a classical liberal who took part in agitation for a constitution and reforms.

Marx was the third of nine children and became the eldest son when his brother Moritz died in 1819. He was baptised into the Lutheran Church on 28 August 1824. His father educated him privately until 1830, when he entered the Gymnasium zu Trier. Its headmaster, Hugo Wyttenbach, employed many liberal humanists, and in 1832 police raided the school and found literature promoting political liberalism among the students. Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841, then turned to radical journalism.

In Paris Marx wrote his Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and began a close collaboration with Friedrich Engels. After moving to Brussels they were active in the Communist League. In London Marx wrote the Grundrisse notebooks and the three volumes of Das Kapital, the second and third of which Engels published after his death, in 1885 and 1894. He became a leading figure in the International Workingmen's Association, and in 1875 wrote the Critique of the Gotha Programme.

His thought drew on Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel's dialectic, on the classical political economy of Adam Smith and David Ricardo, and on French socialist thought. Unlike Hegel, who saw spirit driving history, Marx argued for the primacy of matter over idea. He held that societies develop through class conflict, in capitalism between the bourgeoisie who control the means of production and the proletariat who sell their labour power for wages, and he criticised utopian socialists for relying on small-scale communities.

Marx died on 14 March 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery. His ideas had a profound impact on world politics after the Russian Revolution of 1917. His followers have often disagreed over how to interpret him, and tendencies including Leninism, Marxism–Leninism, Trotskyism, Maoism and Luxemburgism each claim to be his most accurate interpreter. In scholarship his work contributed to the birth of modern sociology, and Isaiah Berlin considered him the true founder of the discipline in so far as anyone can claim the title.
karlsruhe: Karlsruhe lies on the right bank of the Upper Rhine, near the French border, between the Mannheim-Ludwigshafen conurbation to the north and Strasbourg to the south. It stands almost wholly on the Upper Rhine Plain, with the Turmberg to the east and the borders of the Kraichgau, which leads to the northern Black Forest. Its climate is oceanic and its winters are milder than those of most German cities.

According to legend, the name Karlsruhe, meaning Charles's repose or Charles's peace, was given when Margrave Charles III William of Baden-Durlach woke from a dream in which he saw himself founding a new city, after a hunting trip. A variation says that he built the new palace to find peace from his wife. The palace was built in 1715, and a settlement grew around it, for which a mayor was appointed from 1718. From 1812 the mayors bore the title of Lord Mayor.

Karlsruhe was the capital of the Margraviate of Baden-Durlach from 1718 to 1771, of the Margraviate of Baden from 1771 to 1803, of the Electorate of Baden from 1803 to 1806, of the Grand Duchy of Baden from 1806 to 1918 and of the Republic of Baden from 1918 to 1945. It became a major city in the 19th century.

Jews settled there soon after its founding, attracted by the privileges the founder offered to settlers without distinction of creed, and several Jewish families are recorded in 1717. On 9 to 10 November 1938 one synagogue was burned and another damaged, and deportations began on 22 October 1940, when 893 Jews were sent to the Gurs camp in France. Of the 1,280 Jews deported directly from Karlsruhe, 1,175 perished. A new community formed after the war and built a synagogue in 1971.

After the Second World War the provinces of Baden and Württemberg were merged, and Stuttgart became the capital of the new state. In compensation Karlsruhe applied to become the seat of the highest courts.

Karlsruhe is the third-largest city of Baden-Württemberg, with about 310,000 inhabitants, and the seat of the Federal Constitutional Court and the Federal Court of Justice. The palace houses the Baden State Museum. The Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, which grew from the University of Karlsruhe, is the oldest technical university in Germany, and the Centre for Art and Media (ZKM) opened in a former weapons factory in 1999.
karnak: The Karnak Temple Complex is a mixture of temples, pylons, chapels and other buildings near Luxor. The ancient Egyptians called the area Ipet-isut, the Most Select of Places, and it was the main place of worship of the Theban Triad of the 18th Dynasty, headed by the god Amun. The complex has four main parts: the Precinct of Amun-Re, the largest, the Precinct of Mut, the Precinct of Montu and the dismantled Temple of Amenhotep IV. Its distinctive feature is the length of time over which it was built and used. About thirty pharaohs contributed to it, from Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom into the Ptolemaic Kingdom, although most surviving buildings date from the New Kingdom.

Major building in the Precinct of Amun-Re took place in the Eighteenth Dynasty, when Thebes became the capital of the unified country. Thutmose I raised an enclosure wall between the Fourth and Fifth pylons, the earliest part still standing in place. Hatshepsut restored the Precinct of Mut and erected twin obelisks at the temple entrance; one still stands, the second-tallest ancient obelisk standing anywhere. She also built the Red Chapel, intended as a barque shrine.

The Great Hypostyle Hall, begun perhaps in the Eighteenth Dynasty, was mostly built under Seti I and Ramesses II. It covers 5,000 square metres and has 134 columns in 16 rows. Merneptah recorded his victories over the Sea Peoples on the walls of the Cachette Court. Amenhotep IV, Akhenaten, built a temple east of the main complex that was destroyed immediately after his death, so thoroughly that its layout is unknown. Nectanebo I of the Thirtieth Dynasty added the First Pylon and the massive enclosure walls. By the 4th century CE Karnak was mostly abandoned, and Christian churches were founded among the ruins.

In medieval Europe the exact place of Thebes was unknown. The first European description of the complex was by an unknown Venetian in 1589, and the name Karnak is first attested in 1668, when the Capuchin brothers Protais and Charles François d'Orléans travelled through the area. The first drawing is in Paul Lucas's account of 1704. Scientists of the Napoleon expedition, among them Vivant Denon, described it in 1798 and 1799. Karnak was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 with the rest of Thebes.
karnataka: Karnataka lies on the south-western coast of India, bordered by the Lakshadweep Sea to the west and by Goa, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. It has three principal zones: the coastal region of Karavali and Tulu Nadu, the hilly Malenadu region of the Western Ghats, and the Bayaluseeme plains of the Deccan Plateau, where most of the state lies. Its two main river systems are the Krishna and its tributaries in the north and the Kaveri and its tributaries in the south. Most rivers flow east to the Bay of Bengal, while the Sharavati and Netravati flow west.

The name is generally derived from the Kannada words karu and nādu, meaning elevated land. It may also be read as black region, after the black cotton soil of the Bayaluseeme. The British used Carnatic, sometimes Karnatak, for both sides of peninsular India south of the Krishna.

Karnataka's prehistory goes back to a Paleolithic hand-axe culture, and Neolithic and megalithic cultures are also found there. Gold found at Harappa has been traced to mines in Karnataka, which has led scholars to propose contacts with the Indus Valley Civilisation around 3300 BCE. Before the third century BCE most of the region belonged to the Mauryan Empire of Ashoka, and four centuries of Satavahana rule followed.

The decline of Satavahana power led to the earliest native kingdoms, the Kadambas and the Western Gangas, which marked the region's emergence as an independent political entity. The Kadamba dynasty, founded by Mayurasharma, had its capital at Banavasi, and the Western Ganga dynasty ruled from Talakad. Religious thinkers also shaped the region. Adi Shankara (788–820 CE) chose Sringeri for the first of his four monasteries, and Madhvacharya (1238–1317) taught the Dvaita school of Vedanta. The Haridasa devotional movement shaped the culture of South India over some six centuries.

The state was formed as Mysore State on 1 November 1956 under the States Reorganisation Act and renamed in 1973. Its capital and largest city is Bengaluru, and the 2011 census recorded about 61 million inhabitants in 31 districts. Kannada, one of the classical languages of India, is the principal official language, with Tulu an additional official language. The government has a Legislative Assembly of 224 members and a Legislative Council.

Bandipur and Nagarhole National Parks were included in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve in 1986. Yakshagana, a classical dance drama of the coastal and Malnad regions, is among the major theatrical forms, and the Mysore style of Bharatanatya is also associated with the state.
kars: Kars is the seat of Kars Province and Kars District in north-eastern Turkey. Strabo's geography places it in the ancient region of Chorzene, part of the province of Ayrarat in the Kingdom of Armenia. Its name may derive from the Armenian word hars, meaning bride, or from the Georgian kari, meaning gate. Its winters are freezing, with four months of snow cover on average.

Little is known of Kars's early history, but in medieval times it had its own dynasty of Armenian rulers and was the capital of the region of Vanand. By 888 it belonged to the Armenian Bagratunis, and it was their capital from 929 to 961, when its cathedral, later the Church of the Holy Apostles, was built. In 963 it became the capital of a separate kingdom, still called Vanand. In 1064 its king, Gagik-Abas, paid homage to the Seljuk Turks, and in 1065 he ceded the kingdom to the Byzantine Empire, after which the Seljuks took the city. Zakare of the Zakarids captured it in 1206, the Mongols in 1242, and Timur levelled it in 1387.

Kars then passed between Turkic dynasties and the Safavid dynasty, and the Ottomans took it in 1585. Murad III rebuilt the fortifications, which withstood a siege by Nader Shah in 1731, though Nader Shah routed an Ottoman army there in 1745. Russia took the city in 1828 but returned it. In 1855 the Russians took it after an Ottoman garrison led by British officers, including General William Fenwick Williams, held out through a siege until cholera and hunger forced surrender. The Russians stormed it again in the war of 1877–78 and made it the capital of Kars Oblast.

In the First World War the Ottomans captured Kars in April 1918, and in May 1919 it came under the Armenian Republic as the capital of its Vanand province. Turkish forces under General Kâzım Karabekir took it with little resistance on 30 October 1920. The Treaty of Kars of 23 October 1921, signed by Turkey and the Soviet republics, established Turkey's present north-eastern boundaries. After the Second World War the Soviet Union demanded the region back in 1945 and dropped its claims by 1948.

Kars has a mixed population of Azerbaijanis, Kurds and Turks, and Kafkas University was founded there in 1992. The citadel on its rocky hill has Bagratuni walls on the north side and probably took its present form in the thirteenth century under the Zakarids. Below it stands the former Armenian church of the Holy Apostles, converted to a mosque in 1579 and again in 1993. Russian-era buildings give the city a distinct look, and it is the setting of Orhan Pamuk's novel Snow.
kashgar: Kashgar, also called Kashi in Chinese, lies in the Tarim Basin region of southern Xinjiang, near China's border with Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. For over 2,000 years it has been a strategically important oasis on the Silk Road linking China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. It stands at the convergence of widely different cultures and empires and has been under Chinese, Turkic, Mongol and Tibetan rule. Its earliest recorded names are Shufu and Shule, and Ptolemy calls it Kasi. The name Kashgar did not appear in Chinese records until the Song dynasty.

The earliest mention of Kashgar comes from a Han dynasty envoy who travelled the Northern Silk Road. In 76 BCE the Chinese conquered the Xiongnu, Khotan, Kashgar and other Tarim Basin states. Its people practised Zoroastrianism and Buddhism before Islam. In the Tang period a long struggle began between China and the Western Turks for the basin, and the king of Kashgar sent emissaries to the Tang capital in 635 and 639. The Arabs invaded in 711, but Islam was established at Kashgar only in the 10th century, under the Kara-Khanid Khanate.

Genghis Khan swept away the Kara-Khitai in 1219, and Kashgar then came under the Chagatai Khans. Marco Polo visited the city and recorded numerous Nestorian Christians with their own churches. In the 14th century the Chagataid khan Tughluq Timur converted to Islam. The Qing defeated the Dzungar Khanate and took control of Kashgar in 1759, settling emigrants of other ethnic groups near a Manchu garrison. The Dungan Revolt of 1862 to 1877 reached the Tarim Basin, and in 1864 the people of Kashgar rose against their rulers and called on the Kyrgyz chief Sadik Beg, who was reinforced by Buzurg Khan and his general Yakub Beg.

From 1912 to 1928 Yang Zengxin governed Xinjiang, and the Republic created Shule County at Kashgar in 1913. The British consulate at Chini Bagh watched local developments. In September 1949 the provincial authorities declared their allegiance to the Chinese Communist Party, and units of the People's Liberation Army entered southern Xinjiang, including Kashgar, from October.

Kashgar is a county-level city and the administrative centre of Kashgar Prefecture, which had about 4 million people in 2010. The city had 711,300 inhabitants in 2019. In 1986 the Chinese government designated it a city of historical and cultural significance. It is a terminus of the Karakoram Highway. It has a cool arid climate and is one of the driest cities in the world, with about 85 millimetres of precipitation a year.
kashmir: Kashmir is the northernmost geographical region of the Indian subcontinent. Until the mid-19th century the name meant only the Kashmir Valley between the Great Himalayas and the Pir Panjal Range, and it has since come to include the larger area of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. The earliest text to mention the name is Pāṇini's Ashtadhyayi in the 5th century BCE, which calls the people Kashmirikas. The Ancient Greeks called it Kasperia. In the 11th century the poet Bilhana called it Sharada Desha, land of Sharada, and Kashmir was the seat of Sharada Peeth, a historical centre of learning.

In the first millennium Kashmir became an important centre of Buddhism. The Karakotas, most notably Lalitaditya Muktapida, ruled in the second half of that millennium, followed by the Loharas, and Kashmir Shaivism arose in the ninth century. Hindu rule ended in 1339 when Shah Mir became the first Muslim ruler and founded a dynasty that ruled until 1568, most notably under Zain Ul Abedin. The native Chak dynasty followed, until Akbar conquered the region in 1586. Mughal rule lasted until 1751, followed by the Afghan Durrani Empire, until the Sikhs under Ranjit Singh annexed Kashmir. Sikh rule was generally considered oppressive.

Gulab Singh, anointed Raja of Jammu in 1822, rose in the Sikh court and with his general Zorawar Singh conquered Rajouri, Kishtwar, Kargil, Ladakh and Baltistan, surrounding the valley. After the Sikh defeat in the First Anglo-Sikh War, the British, under the Treaty of Amritsar in 1846, made over to Gulab Singh for 75 lakhs the mountainous country east of the Indus and west of the Ravi, including the Vale of Kashmir. The resulting princely state combined Buddhist Ladakh, mixed Jammu, the overwhelmingly Muslim valley with a small Hindu minority of Kashmiri Pandits, Shia Baltistan and the Gilgit Agency.

When British rule ended in 1947 the ruler, Hari Singh, hesitated over accession, and after a Pakistani-sponsored guerrilla onslaught he appealed for help and acceded to India on the condition of Indian military aid. A ceasefire under United Nations auspices was agreed at the end of 1948. The region is divided among three countries: India administers Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, Pakistan administers Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and China administers Aksai Chin and the Trans-Karakoram Tract. Neither India nor Pakistan has formally recognised the accession of the areas the other claims. The two countries fought further wars over the territory in 1965 and 1999.
kassaman: Under French rule the native population of Algeria was given very few political rights for a century. A nationalist movement began in the 1920s and gained strength after World War II, when a government commitment to grant French Algeria autonomy failed to materialise. A prominent member of the movement was Moufdi Zakaria, a Mozabite Berber poet affiliated with the Algerian People's Party. He was jailed and tortured on several occasions between the 1920s and 1962.

He wrote the words in April 1955, during one of these imprisonments, in Barberousse Prison. Since he had no paper or writing instruments, he reportedly wrote the lyrics with his own blood on the walls of his cell. The music was composed by the Egyptian composer Mohamed Fawzi, who was asked to take on the task after two earlier submissions by other composers, one of them by Mohamed Triki, had been rejected.

The lyrics read as a war song. They promote nationalist ideals on the front line, glorify the actions of the National Liberation Front and present armed uprising as the only route to independence. The song alludes to France, the former colonial ruler, in connection with the violent struggle for independence, and foretells that a day of reckoning will come for it. Usually only the first verse is performed, for brevity, as at sporting events.

The words and music were officially adopted in 1962, the year in which the Évian Accords were signed. They paved the way for a referendum in which Algerians voted overwhelmingly for independence, which was then granted. Although Kassaman was intended only as a provisional national anthem, it has endured. In November 2008 an amendment to Article 5 of the Constitution of Algeria declared it immutable, given its association with the country's revolution, and confirmed that the anthem comprises all of its verses, ending the discussion of whether the unfavourable reference to France was still appropriate.
kassel: Kassel lies on both sides of the Fulda River in northern Hesse. It was first mentioned in 913, when King Conrad I signed two deeds there, in a place called Chasella or Chassalla, a fortification at a bridge over the Fulda. The origin of the name is unproven: it may come from the ancient Castellum Cattorum, a castle of the Chatti, or from words meaning a valley and a hall. A deed of 1189 shows that Cassel had city rights, though the date they were granted is not known. The first castle was built in 1277 and later replaced by a Renaissance palace that burned down in 1811.

In 1567 the Landgraviate of Hesse, until then centred in Marburg, was divided among four sons, and Kassel became the capital of Hesse-Kassel and a centre of Calvinist Protestantism in Germany. Strong fortifications protected the Protestant stronghold, and the Rosicrucian Fama Fraternitatis was first published there in 1617. In 1685 Landgrave Charles gave refuge to 1,700 Huguenots, in the new borough of Oberneustadt. In the late 18th century Hesse-Kassel sold auxiliary troops to the British crown to help suppress the American Revolution, and the money financed palaces. The Brothers Grimm lived in Kassel in the early 19th century, where they collected and wrote most of their fairy tales.

Napoleon annexed the Electorate, and Kassel was the capital of the Kingdom of Westphalia under his brother Jérôme from 1807. The Electorate was restored in 1813 and annexed by Prussia in 1866, after it sided with Austria in the Austro-Prussian War. Kassel then ceased to be a princely residence but became an industrial centre and railway junction, home of Henschel & Son, the largest locomotive maker in Germany at the end of the 19th century. After the Battle of Sedan in 1870 Napoleon III was held prisoner at Wilhelmshöhe Palace.

In the Second World War a subcamp of Dachau provided forced labour for the Henschel works, which included tank plants. The heaviest bombing destroyed 90 per cent of the downtown area, killed some 10,000 people and left 150,000 homeless. The US 80th Infantry Division took the city in house-to-house fighting from 1 to 4 April 1945. Most old buildings in the centre were not restored, and large parts of the inner city were rebuilt in the style of the 1950s, though the Museum Fridericianum was restored. Kassel had 201,048 inhabitants in December 2020 and has a university. The Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the documenta exhibitions of contemporary art are held there.
kathiawar: The peninsula covers about 61,000 square kilometres and faces the Arabian Sea on the south and south-west. From the heads of its two gulfs the Little Rann of Kutch and the waste tracts of Khambhat, half salt morass and half sandy desert, reach inland towards each other, so that only one narrow neck on the north-east joins Kathiawar to the mainland of Gujarat. Two belts of hill country cross it, and nine rivers drain it radially; they carry little water outside the monsoon months, and dams have been built on some of them. Most of the natural vegetation is dry scrub. The region has also been called Sorath.

The name Kathiawad seems to derive from the early settlements of the Kathis, who entered Gujarat from Sindh in the early centuries of the Common Era; Saurashtra comes from Sanskrit words meaning good nation. In the reign of Chandragupta Maurya the region was governed by Pushyagupta, and under Ashoka by the Yavana Tushaspa. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, of the first century CE, calls the coast Syrastrene and describes a fertile country yielding wheat, rice, sesame oil, clarified butter and cotton cloth, with many cattle. The Junagadh rock inscription attributed to Rudradaman I, dated to 150 CE, also mentions the region.

After Indian independence in 1947, 217 princely states of Kathiawar, among them the former Junagadh State, were merged on 15 February 1948 into the United State of Kathiawar, renamed Saurashtra State in November 1948. Vallabhbhai Patel spent much time persuading the princes; Maharaja Krishnakumar Sinhji of Bhavnagar State was the first to offer his state. Rajkot was the capital and Uchharangray Navalshankar Dhebar the first chief minister. On 1 November 1956 Saurashtra was merged into Bombay state, and when that state was divided along linguistic lines in 1960 it became part of Gujarat.

The region now comprises eleven districts of Gujarat, with part of Ahmedabad district; historically it also took in Diu. Gir National Park and its surroundings hold the last remaining population of Asiatic lions, and the peninsula has two further national parks, the Blackbuck National Park at Velavadar and the Marine National Park in the Gulf of Kutch. Severe droughts have repeatedly left farmers without crops or drinking water. A campaign to build check dams from the late 1990s raised water tables, but in 2019 a severe drought struck again and water had to be brought by tanker from the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River.
kathmandu: Kathmandu lies in the northwestern part of the Kathmandu Valley, north of the Bagmati River, at an elevation of about 1,324 metres. The city covers 50.7 square kilometres and is bounded by Lalitpur, also called Patan, with which it forms one urban area surrounded by a ring road. It is dissected by eight rivers, of which the main one is the Bagmati. The valley is an ancient lake basin with fertile soil and flat terrain, which helped form a society based on agriculture.

Its position between India and China made it an important trading centre. Trade flourished along an offshoot of the Silk Road linking India and Tibet, and Lhasa Newar merchants of Kathmandu conducted trade across the Himalaya and helped spread art styles and Buddhism across Central Asia.

Archaeological excavations in Kathmandu have found evidence of ancient civilisations. The oldest finding is a statue from Maligaon dated to 185 CE. The excavation of Dhando Chaitya uncovered a brick with an inscription in Brahmi script, which archaeologists believe is two thousand years old. Historically the valley was known as the Nepal Mandala and was the cultural and political hub of the Newar people. From ancient times until the medieval period Kathmandu was known as Kantipur, which derives from Sanskrit words meaning beauty and place, giving the sense of city of light.

The name Kathmandu comes from Kasthamandap, a public pavilion made of wood, from the Sanskrit words for wood and pavilion. It was rebuilt in 1596 in the period of King Lakshmi Narasimha Malla, and according to legend all its timber came from a single tree. The earliest Western reference to the city is in the account of the Portuguese Jesuit Father Joao Cabral, who passed through the valley in the spring of 1628 and was received by the king, probably Lakshminarasimha Malla. He reported that they reached Cadmendu, the capital of the kingdom of Nepal.

Kathmandu is the capital and largest city of Nepal and its main governmental, financial, industrial and cultural centre. The 2021 census recorded a population of 845,767, with approximately 4 million in the surrounding metropolitan area. Its people are multi-ethnic, with a Hindu majority and a significant Vajrayana Buddhist presence. Since 1985 it has hosted the headquarters of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation.

Hindu and Buddhist practice has influenced the monuments of the city over the centuries. In 2006 UNESCO declared seven groups of monuments in the valley a World Heritage Site, among them Durbar Square, Swayambhu Mahachaitya, Bouddha and Pashupatinath.
kathmandu-valley: The Kathmandu Valley is a bowl-shaped valley in the Himalayan mountains of Nepal, at the crossroads of ancient civilisations of the Indian subcontinent and the wider Asian continent. Historically the valley and adjoining areas formed a confederation known as the Nepal Mandala. Until the 15th century Bhaktapur was its capital, when Kathmandu and Lalitpur were established as two further capitals. The name Kathmandu comes from Kasthamandap, a wooden pavilion in Kathmandu Durbar Square built in 1596 by King Lakshmi Narasimha Malla, said to contain no iron nails or supports.

The Newars are the indigenous inhabitants and the creators of the valley's historic civilisation, and their language is Newar, not to be confused with Nepali. The valley's trademark is the multiple-roofed pagoda, which may have originated there. A Newar artisan, Araniko, travelled to the court of Kublai Khan in the 13th century and influenced styles in China and Tibet.

The valley's origin is explained in legend. According to the Swayambhu Purana it was once a lake called Nagahrada, inhabited by Nagas. Vipassi Buddha planted a lotus seed in it, which grew into a radiant manifestation of the primordial Buddha called Svayambhu, and the bodhisattva Manjushri drained the lake by cutting a gorge. In a Hindu account Krishna drained the lake by cutting through the southern hills with his Sudarshana Chakra.

Kathmandu, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur and a ring of smaller cities form the largest urban agglomeration in Nepal, with about 5 million people. The valley has at least 130 important monuments, including pilgrimage sites for Hindus and Buddhists. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1979, with seven component sites, among them Pashupatinath Temple, Boudhanath Stupa and Swayambhunath.
katsushika-hokusai: Hokusai's date of birth is unclear but is often given as 31 October 1760, in the Katsushika district of Edo. It is believed his father was Nakajima Ise, a mirror-maker for the shōgun. He began painting around the age of six. At twelve he was sent to work in a bookshop and lending library, at fourteen he became an apprentice to a woodcarver, and at eighteen he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō, a master of ukiyo-e, which then concentrated on courtesans and kabuki actors. He published his first prints, of kabuki actors, in 1779.

After Shunshō's death in 1793 Hokusai explored other styles, including European ones known to him from French and Dutch copper engravings, and was expelled from the Katsukawa school by Shunkō, the chief disciple. In his own words, the embarrassment he suffered at Shunkō's hands motivated the development of his style. He turned from actors and courtesans to landscapes and the daily life of people of many social levels, a breakthrough for ukiyo-e. He used at least thirty names in his lifetime.

By 1800 he had taken the name Katsushika Hokusai, meaning north studio, in honour of the North Star, a symbol of a deity in his Nichiren Buddhism, and he published two collections of landscapes. He taught about 50 pupils over his life. On 5 October 1817 he painted the Great Daruma, 18 by 10.8 metres, in Nagoya before a large crowd. Between 1804 and 1815 he illustrated books with the novelist Takizawa Bakin.

In 1811 he took the name Taito. The first volume of the Hokusai Manga, a collection of drawings of objects, plants, animals and ordinary people, appeared in 1814 and was an immediate success; by 1820 twelve volumes had been produced. After 1820, as Iitsu, he made Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji in the early 1830s, including The Great Wave off Kanagawa. From 1834, as Gakyō Rōjin Manji, the Old Man Mad About Art, he produced One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji.

A fire in 1839 destroyed Hokusai's studio and much of his work,. At 83 he went to Obuse in Shinano Province at the invitation of a wealthy farmer, and he kept working almost until the end. He died on 10 May 1849 and was buried at the Seikyō-ji in Tokyo. Hokusai's prints were collected by European artists including Degas, Gauguin, Manet and van Gogh. Claude Debussy is believed to have been inspired by The Great Wave in La Mer, which first appeared in 1905.
kauai: Kauaʻi has an area of 1,456 square kilometres, making it the fourth largest of the Hawaiian Islands, and lies 117 kilometres northwest of Oʻahu across the Kauaʻi Channel. It is about five million years old, the oldest of the main islands, though Niʻihau is older. Its highest peak is Kawaikini at 1,598 metres, and Mount Waiʻaleʻale, 1,569 metres high, has an average annual rainfall of 11.7 metres on its east side, one of the wettest spots on earth. Rain has carved deep valleys and canyons with many waterfalls, and the flow of the Waimea River formed Waimea Canyon, about 910 metres deep.

It is uncertain when people first reached the Hawaiian Islands. Early archaeological studies suggested that Polynesian explorers from the Marquesas or Society Islands arrived as early as 600 CE, with a second wave from Tahiti around 1100, while later analyses suggest the first settlers came between 900 and 1200. Kauaʻi had its own dialect of Hawaiian, which still survives on Niʻihau.

In January 1778 the British navigator James Cook arrived at Kauaʻi by accident during his third voyage, the first recorded contact between a European and the indigenous people of the islands. By 1795 Kamehameha I had united most of the islands in the Kingdom of Hawaii, but Kauaʻi stayed independent. His attempt to conquer it in 1796 was cancelled because of stormy seas, and a second invasion planned from Oʻahu was cancelled after an epidemic broke out among his forces. In 1810 Kaumualiʻi, who had ruled Kauaʻi since 1803, agreed to be Kamehameha's vassal and to cede the island on his death by making Kamehameha's son his heir.

In 1816 Georg Anton Schäffer, a German working for the Russian-American Company, involved Kaumualiʻi in a plan to place Kauaʻi under the protection of the Russian Empire, and a fort was built at Waimea in 1817. On Kamehameha's orders Kaumualiʻi dismissed the Russians. From 1835 sugarcane plantations were the island's most important industry for about a century; the last, the Gay & Robinson Plantation, stopped planting in 2008.

Kauaʻi calls itself the Garden Isle and holds Waimea Canyon State Park and Nā Pali Coast State Park. It forms most of Kauaʻi County, which also includes Niʻihau, Kaʻula and Lehua, and its population was 73,298 in 2020.
kaunas: Kaunas stands at the confluence of Lithuania's two largest rivers, the Nemunas and the Neris, near the Kaunas Reservoir, the largest body of water in the country. Its name is of Lithuanian origin and most likely derives from the personal name of an unknown ruler of the castle, a name taken from an adjective meaning one who likes to fight. A 16th-century legend in the Bychowiec Chronicle instead says that it was founded by Romans led by a patrician named Palemon, who fled from the Emperor Nero, and that his son Kunas built a fortress at the confluence.

A settlement stood on the site of the Old Town by the 10th century at the latest. Kaunas was first mentioned in written sources in 1361. The brick Kaunas Castle defended its residents against the Teutonic Order, and with the castle at Grodno it was one of only two brick castles on the Nemunas, which was the main front line between the Crusaders and the Lithuanians. In 1408 Vytautas the Great granted Kaunas city rights and chose its coat of arms, which shows an aurochs. After the third partition of the Polish–Lithuanian state in 1795 the city passed to the Russian Empire, and Napoleon's Grand Army passed through it twice in 1812, devastating it both times.

After Vilnius was occupied by the Red Army in 1919, the Lithuanian government made Kaunas its main base, and it became the temporary capital when Vilnius was annexed by Poland. It held that position until 28 October 1939. In June 1940 the Soviet Union occupied and annexed Lithuania. On 29 June 1941 over 9,200 Jews were murdered in the Kaunas pogrom, and nearly 50,000 people, over 30,000 of them Jews, were killed at the Ninth Fort during the Nazi occupation. The Red Army took the city on 1 August 1944, and the region became a centre of the partisan war against Soviet rule, which ended by 1953.

Kaunas is the second-largest city in Lithuania after Vilnius and the capital of Kaunas County. It is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Kaunas. The interwar city was known for its Art Deco and Lithuanian National Revival architecture, and in 2023 it became a World Heritage Site.
kayseri: The city lies on a low spur at the foot of Mount Erciyes, a dormant volcano that rises to 3,917 metres, more than 1,500 metres above the city's mean altitude. In antiquity the mountain was Mount Argaeus. The site stood at a crossing of trade routes: that from Sinope to the Euphrates, and the Persian Royal Road from Sardis to Susa during more than two centuries of Achaemenid rule. In Roman times a route from Ephesus to the east crossed it as well.

Kayseri has been equated with the early Hittite kingdom of Kussara, mentioned in early Assyrian trading records, and a first period of prosperity is dated to about 2000 BCE, when it served as a trading post between Assyrians and Hittites. As Mazaca it was the residence of the kings of Cappadocia. According to Armenian tradition it was founded by Mishak. In 14 CE the last king, Archelaus, renamed it Caesarea in Cappadocia in honour of Augustus. In the fourth century Basil of Caesarea founded there a large complex of charitable institutions, a monastery and churches, known as the Basiliad.

From the mid-seventh century Arab attacks on Cappadocia became common and the city was besieged several times; Muawiyah took it temporarily in 647. The Seljuk ruler Alp Arslan demolished the city and massacred its population in 1067, and it stood uninhabited for about half a century. The Danishmendids rebuilt it in 1134. Under the Sultanate of Rum, from 1178 to 1243, it was one of the sultanate's most important centres, until it fell to the Mongols in 1243. In 1277 Sultan Baybars, after his victory at Elbistan, entered the city and massacred its Christians while sparing the Muslim inhabitants. The Eretnids held it in the fourteenth century and the Ottomans took it in 1515.

The Seljuk period left the Hunat Hatun Complex, the Kiliç Arslan Mosque, the Grand Mosque and the Gevher Nesibe hospital. The Grand Mosque was begun by the Danishmend emir Melik Mehmed Gazi and finished by the Seljuks. During the Turkish War of Independence the building of the Kayseri Lyceum housed the Turkish Grand National Assembly while the Greek army advanced on Ankara.

Kayseri is the capital of Kayseri province in Central Anatolia. Its huge basalt walls, dating to the reign of Justinian in the sixth century, were repeatedly repaired by Seljuks, Ottomans and later authorities. The suburb of Talas was the ancestral home of Calouste Gulbenkian, Aristotle Onassis and Elia Kazan, and the architect Mimar Sinan was born in 1490 at Ağırnas nearby. The archaeological site of Kanesh-Kültepe lies 20 km to the north-east. Public investment in the 1920s and 1930s brought a textile factory and an aircraft factory to the city, and its merchants later built an industrial base.
kazan: Kazan lies at the confluence of the Volga and the Kazanka rivers. In Tatar a kazan is a cauldron, and the name perhaps describes the topographic basin around the city. Its central part is divided by the Bolaq canal and Kaban Lakes into two districts: the Kazan Posad, historically Russian, on the hill, and the Old Tatar Quarter, historically Tatar, between the canal and the Volga, where the mosques stand. Its symbol is Zilant, a mythical dragon-like creature, and the first official coat of arms was approved on 18 October 1781.

According to the official version adopted today, the city is more than 1,000 years old, with an estimated date of the urban settlement of 1004 to 1005. The dating rests on finds in the Kazan Kremlin, among them a Czech coin, remains of masonry and a wooden city fence, and handicrafts.

In 1552 Tsar Ivan the Terrible conquered the city after a siege. During the governorship of Alexander Gorbaty-Shuysky most of the Tatar residents were forcibly Christianised or deported, and mosques and palaces were ruined. The survivors were moved 50 kilometres away, and Tatars in Russian service were settled in the Tatar Bistäse near the city wall. Several great fires destroyed much of the city, and after one of them, in 1579, the icon Our Lady of Kazan was discovered there.

In 1708 the Tsardom of Kazan was abolished and Kazan became the seat of Kazan Governorate. After a visit by Peter the Great it became a centre of shipbuilding for the Caspian fleet. Pugachev's Rebellion, which began in 1773, seized and largely destroyed the city, which was rebuilt under Catherine the Great.

In 1918 Kazan was the capital of the Idel-Ural State, which the Bolshevik government suppressed, and in August of that year the Czechoslovak Legions briefly occupied it. In 1920 it became the centre of the Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. From the Treaty of Rapallo of 1922 until 1933 the German and Russian armies jointly ran the Kama tank school there.

Kazan is the capital and largest city of Tatarstan, with over 1.3 million inhabitants, and the most populous city on the Volga. It is known for the mix of Tatar and Russian cultures. The Kazan Kremlin, a citadel declared a World Heritage Site in 2000, holds the five-domed Annunciation Cathedral of 1561 to 1562 and the Söyembikä Tower, named after the last queen of Kazan.
kerala: Kerala is mainly a strip of coastal plains wedged between the Western Ghats and the Laccadive Sea, 38,863 square kilometres in area, with Karnataka to the northeast and Tamil Nadu to the east. Geographically it falls into three regions: the cool eastern highlands, the central midlands of rolling hills and the western coastal lowlands.

In Hindu tradition the land was won from the sea by the sage Parashurama, the sixth avatar of Vishnu, who threw his axe across the water so that the sea withdrew to where it landed. Archaeology shows Neolithic dolmens in the Marayur region and rock engravings in the Edakkal caves in Wayanad from about 6000 BCE. Sumerian records are said to show Kerala as a spice exporter from at least 3000 BCE, and Babylonians, Assyrians and Egyptians were drawn to the Malabar Coast in the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, as were Arabs and Phoenicians.

The word Kerala first appears as Keralaputra, son of the Cheras, in an edict of the Maurya emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. The Cheras were the earliest major dynasty of the region and rose through maritime commerce, but often faced invasion from the Chola and Pandya dynasties. A second Chera kingdom, c. 800 to 1102, was founded by Kulasekhara Varman and governed most of present-day Kerala and parts of Tamil Nadu, with a flourishing of art, literature, trade and the Bhakti movement. Most historians hold that Malayalam descends from a dialect of early middle Tamil and became a distinct language between the 9th and 13th centuries.

Vasco da Gama arrived at Kappad, near Kozhikode, in 1498, and the Zamorin of Kozhikode allowed the Portuguese to trade, which led to a factory and fort. In 1947 the princely states of Travancore and Kochi acceded to India, and on 1 July 1949 they merged as Travancore-Cochin. On 1 November 1956 the Malabar district and the Kasargod taluk were joined to it, and its four southern taluks went to Madras State, forming Kerala under the States Reorganisation Act. The first elections in 1957 produced a Communist-led government under E. M. S. Namboodiripad, among the earliest democratically elected Communist governments in the world.

Kerala is a state of southern India with its capital at Thiruvananthapuram, and 33 million people at the census of 2011. Malayalam is the most widely spoken language and, with English, an official one. Hinduism is practised by more than 54 per cent of the people, followed by Islam and Christianity.
kharkiv: Kharkiv stands on the banks of the Kharkiv, Lopan and Udy rivers, which flow into the Siverskyi Donets watershed in north-eastern Ukraine. It is the main city of the historic region of Sloboda Ukraine, also called Slobozhanshchyna. The name probably comes from the river Kharkiv, which is attested earlier than the fortress; a folk etymology connects it to a Cossack founder called Kharko.

The earliest historical references to the region are to Scythian and Sarmatian settlement in the 2nd century BCE. In the 8th to 10th centuries the Khazar fortress of Verkhneye Saltovo stood about 40 km east of the modern city. In the 12th century the area belonged to the Cumans, and from the mid-13th century to the Golden Horde. In 1654 settlers arrived on the banks of the Lopan and Kharkiv rivers and rebuilt and fortified an abandoned settlement. In 1765 Kharkiv became the seat of a separate Sloboda Ukraine Governorate, and an imperial university was decreed in January 1805.

In December 1919 the Bolsheviks made Kharkiv the capital of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. Ukrainian replaced Russian as the largest recorded nationality, though Russian remained the dominant spoken language. In the 1930s the city was a centre of Ukrainian writing, nicknamed a Literary Klondike, and over 100 of these writers were repressed in the Stalinist purges, an event called the Executed Renaissance. German forces occupied Kharkiv from 1941, with an interval in 1943, and under their rule its Jewish population was systematically destroyed. The city was liberated on 23 August 1943. In the referendum of 1 December 1991, 86 per cent of Kharkiv Oblast approved Ukrainian statehood.

Kharkiv is the second-largest city of Ukraine and the administrative centre of Kharkiv Oblast, with a population of 1,430,885 in 2023. Machinery, electronics and military hardware have been its leading industries, and it has many research institutes. Principal landmarks include the Dormition Cathedral, built in the 1680s and rebuilt in the 1820s and 1830s, the Annunciation Cathedral, completed on 2 October 1888, the Derzhprom building in Freedom Square and the Kharkiv Railway Station.
khartoum: Khartoum stands at the confluence of the White Nile, flowing north from Lake Victoria, and the Blue Nile, flowing west from Lake Tana in Ethiopia. The meeting place is known as al-Mogran. The two rivers divide the metropolitan area into three parts: Khartoum proper, Khartoum North and Omdurman, linked by bridges. The site is flat, at about 385 metres above sea level, with a hot desert climate and a very short rainy season. One proposed origin of the name is the Arabic khurṭūm, trunk, probably for the strip of land between the rivers.

Khartoum was established in 1821, 24 km north of the ancient city of Soba, as an outpost of the Egyptian army, soon after Muhammad Ali Pasha had incorporated Sudan into his realm. Egypt moved its colonial government there in 1823, and the settlement grew into a regional centre of trade on the caravan route from Ethiopia to Egypt and a focus of the slave trade. Floods destroyed most of the city in 1854, and it was rebuilt in mud and stone instead of thatch and straw.

The Siege of Khartoum began on 13 March 1884, when troops of the Mahdi, Muhammad Ahmad, besieged the Egyptian garrison under the British General Charles George Gordon. The Mahdists took the city on 26 January 1885 and annihilated the garrison. Many inhabitants were massacred or enslaved, the survivors were deported to the newly founded Omdurman, and Khartoum was largely destroyed and abandoned.

After the reconquest of 1898 Khartoum became the capital of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. Herbert Kitchener, Governor-General from September 1898, rebuilt it on a street plan in the shape of the Union Jack. The Gordon Memorial College opened in 1903, and a railway to Port Sudan was completed in 1919. Khartoum became the capital of independent Sudan in 1956.

Khartoum is the capital and most populous city of Sudan, and Greater Khartoum is the country's largest urban area. It is an economic and trade centre with rail lines from Port Sudan, El Obeid and Wadi Halfa. The National Museum of Sudan, founded in 1971, holds two Egyptian temples, from Buhen and Semna, moved there when Lake Nasser was flooded. The city also has the Khalifa House Museum and the University of Khartoum, and it saw heavy fighting and destruction in the civil war that began in April 2023.
kiel: Kiel lies on the Kieler Förde, an inlet of the Bay of Kiel, in the southeast of the Jutland Peninsula, at the mouth of the Schwentine River and about 90 kilometres northeast of Hamburg. The Kiel Canal, which joins the Baltic to the North Sea, has one end in the district of Holtenau and the other at Brunsbüttel. Most of the city belongs to Holstein, while the districts north of the canal are historically part of Southern Schleswig.

Count Adolf IV of Holstein founded the city in 1233 as Holstenstadt tom Kyle, and his eldest son, John I of Schauenburg, granted it Lübeck city rights in 1242. As capital of the county, later the duchy, of Holstein, it belonged to the Holy Roman Empire. It was a member of the Hanseatic League from 1284 until it was expelled in 1518 for harbouring pirates. Kiel University was founded in 1665 by Christian Albert, Duke of Holstein-Gottorp.

From 1773 to 1864 the town belonged to the king of Denmark, who ruled Holstein through a personal union. After the Second Schleswig War of 1864 it was administered briefly by Austria and Prussia, and the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 led to its annexation by Prussia. King William I moved Prussia's Baltic fleet there on 24 March 1865, and as Germany's main naval base the city grew from 18,770 people in 1864 to about 200,000 in 1910.

In late 1918 the fleet stationed at Kiel was ordered to sail for a last battle with the Royal Navy. The sailors, who thought it a suicide mission, refused, took over Kiel and spread the revolt to other northern ports, setting off the revolution that ended the monarchy and created the Weimar Republic. In the Second World War heavy bombing destroyed more than 80 per cent of the remaining old town. British forces seized the city on 5 May 1945, and in 1946 it was named capital of the new state of Schleswig-Holstein.

Kiel is the capital and most populous city of Schleswig-Holstein and Germany's largest city on the Baltic Sea. Its oldest building is the 13th-century Church of St. Nicholas. The shipyard Howaldtswerke-Deutsche Werft, founded in 1838, built the first German submarine, the Brandtaucher, in 1850.
kigali: Kigali lies near the geographic centre of Rwanda, in rolling hills of valleys and ridges joined by steep slopes. Its name comes from the Kinyarwanda prefix ki- and the suffix -gali, meaning wide or broad, and was first applied to Mount Kigali. According to oral history the name dates from the 14th century, when King Cyilima I Rugwe is said to have viewed the territory from a hill and called the country vast. The central business district stands on Nyarugenge Hill, the site of the original settlement.

According to oral history the Kingdom of Rwanda was founded in the 14th century on the shores of Lake Muhazi, about 40 kilometres east of the present city. The early kingdom included Kigali, but it was a small state with larger neighbours, Bugesera and Gisaka. The scholar Alexis Kagame proposed that Kigali was made a capital under Cyilima I Rugwe, but there is little direct evidence, and the later pre-colonial kings are known to have been based at Nyanza.

The founding of the city is generally dated to 1907, when the German administrator and explorer Richard Kandt, the first resident of Rwanda, chose the site for his headquarters for its central location, views and security. Foreign merchants began trading there in the German period, and Kandt opened government schools for Tutsi students.

Belgium took control of Rwanda and Burundi during the First World War, and Kigali remained the seat of colonial administration for Rwanda while Usumbura was the capital of Ruanda-Urundi. At independence in 1962 it had about 6,000 inhabitants. Nyanza and Butare, then called Astrida, were also considered for the capital, but Kigali was chosen for its more central location. In 1973 a bloodless military coup brought Juvénal Habyarimana to power.

In April 1994 he was killed when his aircraft was shot down near Kigali, and the Rwandan genocide followed, which killed over 500,000 Tutsi. The Rwandan Patriotic Front seized Kigali on 4 July 1994. The city lost a large part of its people to killing and flight, and after 1995 refugees returned and much of it was rebuilt.

Kigali is the capital, largest city and a province-level administrative unit of Rwanda, divided into three districts: Gasabo, Kicukiro and Nyarugenge. It had 1,745,555 inhabitants at the 2022 census. It is the country's economic and financial hub and its main port of entry, and houses the president's residence and most government ministries. The Kigali Genocide Memorial hosts the national commemoration on 7 April, and 4 July is observed as Liberation Day. The house in which Kandt lived is now the Kandt House Museum of Natural History.
kigeli-iv-rwabugiri: Rwabugiri, whose birth name is given as Sezisoni Rwabugiri, was a Tutsi of the Nyiginya dynasty, which traced its line back to Gihanga, one of the first kings whose deeds are celebrated in Rwanda's oral chronicles. His year of birth is uncertain and is given as about 1840. He held authority from 1867 to 1895 and was among the last kings of his line.

Around 1870 Rwabugiri established a royal court at Rubengera that collected labour dues and tribute in food. It channelled food across the country and became a centre of commerce. The court managed production so as to keep a surplus as a provision against famine, and on the king's order this was distributed to the poorest in exchange for their labour; in times of shortage, however, the very rich Tutsi living at Rubengera could find food and livestock while most of the country suffered.

As he annexed new lands he placed appointed chiefs over them, drawn into a network that bound the regions to the court. These chiefs sometimes met local resistance: in the north-west the Balera challenged the Nduga whom the court had installed, a contest along lines of clan, since both groups were then counted as Tutsi. Several annexed districts, such as Bugoyi, Bwishaza and Kingogo, had been inhabited entirely by Hutu, and Tutsi moved into them in numbers afterwards. He also killed chiefs of his own Nyiginya lineage who had shown too much independence.

He was the first king of Rwanda to come into contact with Europeans. He built an army equipped with guns obtained from Germans and barred most foreigners, especially Arabs, from the kingdom, defending its borders against neighbouring kingdoms and slave traders. By the end of his rule the country was divided into provinces, districts, hills and neighbourhoods under a hierarchy of chiefs.

Rwanda had been assigned to the German Empire at a conference in Brussels in 1890, but no expedition came until that of Count Gustav Adolf von Götzen in 1894. Rwabugiri died in September 1895 on an expedition in what is now Congo. His son Rutarindwa was proclaimed king as Mibambwe IV, with Kanjogera of the Bega clan, another of Rwabugiri's wives, as queen mother. With her brother Kabare she carried out a coup at Rucunshu in which Rutarindwa was killed, and made her own son king as Yuhi V Musinga. The weakened state opened the way to direct German colonisation in 1897.
kim-il-sung: Kim Il Sung was born Kim Sung Ju on 15 April 1912 near Pyongyang, then called Heijō, to the independence activist Kim Hyong-jik and Kang Pan Sok. He grew up in northeast China. North Korean sources credit him with founding the Down-with-Imperialism Union in 1926, though most scholarly sources reject this. He attended Yuwen Middle School in Jilin until 1930, and at seventeen became the youngest member of the Korean Communist Youth Association, an underground group of fewer than twenty members. Police discovered it three weeks after it formed in 1929 and jailed him for several months. He joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1931 and fought in anti-Japanese guerrilla groups.

In 1942 he was assigned to the Soviet Red Army and stayed in the Soviet Union until 1945. Some sources claim that the name Kim Il Sung had belonged to an earlier resistance leader, Kim Kyung-cheon, but the historian Andrei Lankov has argued that this is unlikely.

Captain Kim Il Sung, a 33-year-old officer of the Red Army, arrived at the port of Wonsan on 19 September 1945 after 26 years in exile. He had only eight years of formal education, all of it in Chinese, and a Soviet officer later said he was essentially created from zero. The Soviet Union designated him premier of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea on 9 September 1948. In June 1949 the Workers' Party of North Korea merged with its southern counterpart to become the Workers' Party of Korea, with Kim as chairman. By 1949 he had consolidated communist rule and begun to promote a personality cult, and the first of many statues of him appeared.

Archival material suggests that the decision to invade South Korea in 1950 was Kim's own initiative, not a Soviet one. A ceasefire was signed in 1953, and the war left North Korea devastated. Kim launched a five-year economic plan on the Soviet model, with state-owned industry and collectivised farming. In 1957 the songbun system divided the population into core, wavering and hostile classes, which decided access to education, housing and employment. In 1966 the promotion of Juche as the state ideology began, and the Monolithic Ideological System was introduced in May 1967. In 1972 North and South Korea signed the July 4 South-North Joint Statement on reunification.

Kim handed the chairmanship of the National Defense Commission to his son Kim Jong Il in 1991 and 1993. He collapsed from a heart attack on 7 July 1994 and died at 2:00 in the morning on 8 July, aged 82; his death was declared 34 hours later. He was succeeded by his son and posthumously declared Eternal President. He had developed Juche, which stressed independence, self-sustenance and self-defence and Korean nationalism.
kim-jong-il: Kim Jong Il was born on 16 February 1941 in the far east of the Soviet Union, generally agreed to be the camp of Voroshilov near Nikolsk. His mother, Kim Jong-suk, was Kim Il Sung's first wife, and the family moved to Pyongyang in 1945. He joined the Workers' Party of Korea in July 1961 and its Propaganda and Agitation Department in 1966.

After the Kapsan faction incident around 1967, the last credible challenge to Kim Il Sung's sole rule, he took part in the investigation and purges that followed, his first official duties. He became director of the department in 1973 and was formally designated his father's successor in October 1980 at the party congress, taking the title Dear Leader as a personality cult was built around him.

Kim Il Sung died on 8 July 1994 and Kim Jong Il became supreme leader. The economy struggled through the 1990s because of mismanagement and severe floods, and North Korea could not import enough to sustain industry, which brought a severe famine. He adopted the Songun, military-first, policy, making the army the central organiser of civil society. In 1996 he launched a purge named the Deepening Group Incident; some 25,000 people are thought to have been purged, about 10,000 of them executed.

South Korea's Sunshine Policy from 1998 led to Kim's meeting with Kim Dae-jung in 2000 and to the Kaesong Industrial Park in 2003, though the sinking of ROKS Cheonan and the bombardment of Yeonpyeong in 2010 ended it. In 2002 the government admitted producing nuclear weapons in violation of the 1994 Agreed Framework with the United States, and it announced an underground nuclear test on 9 October 2006.

After he failed to appear at public events in 2008, observers assumed he was ill, and he began to promote his third son, Kim Jong Un, raising him to high party posts in 2010. Kim Jong Il died of a suspected heart attack on 17 December 2011 while travelling by train, and the government announced it two days later. His funeral took place on 28 December in Pyongyang, and he was declared Eternal General Secretary of the party and Eternal Chairman of the National Defence Commission.
kingston-jamaica: Kingston lies on the south-eastern coast of Jamaica and faces a natural harbour protected by the Palisadoes, a long sand spit that connects the town of Port Royal and the international airport to the rest of the island. The city stands on the Liguanea plain, an alluvial plain beside the Hope River, and is surrounded by the Blue Mountains, the Red Hills, Long Mountain and the harbour. It lies in the rain shadow of the Blue Mountains and is very dry compared with parishes on the windward side. Kingston experiences frequent earthquakes. Two districts make up its central area: the historic Downtown and New Kingston.

Kingston was founded on 22 July 1692, shortly after the earthquake that devastated Port Royal. The original section, at the bottom of the Liguanea Plains, was laid out to house survivors, who first camped on the sea front on Colonel Barry's Hog Crawle; about two thousand people died of mosquito-borne diseases. Before the earthquake its functions had been purely agricultural, and the town did not begin to grow until Port Royal was further destroyed by fire in 1703. The surveyor John Goffe drew up a grid plan bounded by North, East, West and Harbour Streets, with main thoroughfares 66 feet across to ease transport between the port and the plantations inland.

Wolmer's, the first free school, was founded in 1729. By 1780 Kingston had 11,000 inhabitants, and its merchants lobbied for the administrative capital to be moved from Spanish Town, which commercial activity had eclipsed. In 1788 the population was 25,000, about a tenth of the island's; one in four was white, two out of five were free, and the remaining three-fifths were enslaved Black people. The government offices were transferred from Spanish Town in 1872. In 1907 an earthquake killed 800 people and destroyed nearly all the historical buildings south of Parade, and a height limit of 60 feet was then set for buildings in the centre. The island-wide riots of the 1930s led to the growth of trade unions and political parties.

Kingston is the capital and largest city of Jamaica, its main transport hub and its largest seaport. Kingston Harbour is described as the seventh largest natural harbour in the world. The local government bodies of Kingston and St. Andrew were amalgamated in 1923 as the Kingston and St. Andrew Corporation, and the Mona campus of the University of the West Indies was founded in 1948. The majority of the population is of African descent, with minorities including East Indians and Chinese, who came as indentured servants in the late nineteenth century. Kingston hosted the Commonwealth Games in 1966.
kinshasa: Kinshasa stands on the southern shore of Pool Malebo, a widening of the Congo River, in a broad crescent of flat, low-lying terrain at an average elevation of about 300 metres. The city-province covers 9,965 square kilometres, and the Congo River forms its western and northern boundary with the Republic of the Congo. Across the river, about four kilometres away and unbridged, lies Brazzaville, so that the two capitals are the closest pair in the world. The river is a transport route across much of the Congo Basin, with barges navigable between Kinshasa and Kisangani.

The site has been inhabited by Teke and Humbu people for centuries. In pre-colonial times it held two trading centres, Ntamo and Ntsaasa, which were part of the Tio Kingdom. Two theories explain the name Nshasa. One links it to a bag of salt, and to a trading post where people from the lower Congo and the Atlantic exchanged salt for goods including ivory and enslaved people; the other derives it from Teke trading terms, in which fishermen exchanged fish for cassava.

The city was founded on 1 August 1881 as Léopold II Station, and Henry Morton Stanley named it Léopoldville in honour of Leopold II of Belgium. A royal decree of 11 April 1914 designated it the capital of the Belgian Congo, and an ordinance of 25 June 1941 gave it city status. Its population grew from 5,000 in 1889 to 39,530 in 1930 and reached 400,000 at independence in 1960.

In 1966, during Mobutu Sese Seko's Zairianisation campaign, it was renamed Kinshasa as a tribute to the village of Nshasa. Its economic prominence peaked in the 1970s, a period known as la belle époque, and in 1974 it hosted the boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman known as the Rumble in the Jungle.

Kinshasa is the capital and largest city of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with a population estimated at about 18 million. It is also one of the country's 26 provinces, divided into 24 communes. French is the language of government, education and the media, while Lingala is the lingua franca of the street. UNESCO designated it a City of Music in 2015, and it has a long-established music scene and a national stadium, the Stade des Martyrs.
kiribati: Kiribati has a total land area of 811 km2 spread over 3,441,810 km2 of ocean. Its islands, from Banaba in the west to Kiritimati in the east, straddle the equator and the 180th meridian. They fall into three groups: the Gilbert Islands, sixteen atolls about 1,500 km north of Fiji; the Phoenix Islands, eight atolls and coral islands; and the Line Islands, eight atolls and one reef. Banaba is a raised coral island that was once a rich source of phosphates. The rest of the land is sand and reef rock islets that rise only one or two metres above sea level, with thin, calcareous soil. Kiritimati has the largest land area of any atoll in the world.

The area has been inhabited by Austronesian peoples speaking the same Oceanic language since sometime between 3000 BCE and 1300 CE. Oral historians suggest that seafarers from Melanesia came first, later visited by Austronesian seafarers from the west. Around 1300 CE a mass departure from Samoa added Polynesian ancestry and culture. From about the 15th century the northern islands came under chiefly rule (uea), while the central and southern islands were ruled by councils of elders (unimwaane); Tabiteuea alone is known to have kept an egalitarian society. Clans and chiefs fought over land, and some islands used guns and cannon-equipped ships supplied by Europeans to destroy their foes.

The name Gilbert Islands was given around 1820 by the Russian admiral Adam von Krusenstern and the French captain Louis Duperrey, after the British captain Thomas Gilbert, who sighted some of the islands in 1788. The British annexed the Gilberts as a protectorate in 1892. From 1916 the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony took its name from them, and it lasted until the Ellice Islands became Tuvalu in 1976. Kiribati became independent from the United Kingdom in 1979, with the Gilberts, the Phoenix and Line islands and Banaba. The name is the Gilbertese rendering of Gilberts. Phosphate mining on Banaba was exhausted by independence, and the Banabans mostly live on Rabi in Fiji.

Kiribati is a parliamentary democratic republic under the constitution promulgated on 12 July 1979. Its capital, Tarawa, is made up of islets joined by causeways, and more than half the population lives there. A census of November 2020 counted 119,940 people. The I-Kiribati are a Micronesian people who speak Gilbertese, an Oceanic language; English is the other official language. The country joined the United Nations in 1999.
kite: In China the kite has been claimed as the invention of the 5th-century BCE philosophers Mozi and Lu Ban, who flew wooden kites called muyuan. After paper was invented in the Han dynasty, paper kites, called zhiyuan, became popular. Silk for the sail, fine and strong silk for the line and resilient bamboo for the frame were all readily available. By the Tang dynasty, bamboo flutes, whistles and ribbons were attached to kites to make sound, a forerunner of the modern fengzheng, named for that sound. The earliest known Chinese kites were flat and often rectangular, and later tailless kites carried a stabilising bowline. They were decorated with mythological motifs and figures.

Ancient Chinese texts describe kites used for measuring distances, testing the wind, lifting men, signalling and communication in military operations. By 549 a kite was used to carry a message for a rescue mission. During the Song dynasty the Fire Crow, a kite carrying incendiary powder, was made as a weapon. According to the Samguk Sagi, the Korean general Kim Yu-sin of Silla rallied his troops in 647 with flaming kites that also frightened the enemy.

In India the kite evolved into the fighter kite, the patang, and thousands are flown every year at festivals such as Makar Sankranti. Kites were known throughout Polynesia as far as New Zealand, probably carried from China with the people. Polynesian kites of cloth and wood in human form were used in religious ceremonies to send prayers to the gods.

Kites reached Europe late, although the Romans knew windsock-like banners. Marco Polo brought stories of them in the late 13th century, and sailors brought kites back from Japan and Malaysia in the 16th and 17th centuries. Konrad Kyeser described dragon kites in Bellifortis about 1400. At first they were regarded as curiosities, but by the 18th and 19th centuries they served scientific research. Benjamin Franklin published an account of a kite experiment in 1752 to show that lightning was electrical, and kites aided the Wright brothers' research toward the first airplane. The years from 1860 to about 1910 became the European golden age of kiting. Powered aircraft then reduced interest in them.
klagenfurt: Klagenfurt lies in southern Austria near the border with Slovenia, at 446 metres above sea level, on the Wörthersee and the Glan river. To the south the Karawanken range separates Carinthia from Slovenia and Italy. The name means ford of lament. Two Carinthian linguists took it to translate a Slovene name for the neighbouring wetland, a place haunted by a wailing female ghost; a later view derives the Slovene word from an Italic phrase meaning a place at or in the water.

Legend tells that the city was founded after a group of men killed a winged lindwurm that preyed on the duchy from the moors beside the lake. A watchtower was built at the edge of the moor, the dragon was baited with a bull fitted with a chain and hook, and a village arose on the battlefield. The Renaissance monument in the city centre, the Lindwurmbrunnen, commemorates it.

After a great fire Emperor Maximilian I, unable to rebuild the city, ceded Klagenfurt in 1518 to the Estates, the nobility of the duchy, over the protests of the citizens. The new owners dug a canal to the lake to bring timber, built town houses, and enlarged the city on a chequerboard plan following the ideas of the Italian architect Domenico dell'Allio. Fortifications that took half a century to build made it the strongest fortress north of the Alps. French troops under Napoleon destroyed the walls in 1809, and the railway of 1863 strengthened its place as the centre of the region. During the Second World War the city was bombed 41 times, killing 612 people.

Klagenfurt is the capital and largest city of Carinthia and the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Gurk-Klagenfurt. It is regarded as the cultural centre of the Carinthian Slovenes. Its old city has Renaissance arcaded courtyards, the Landhaus, once the palace of the Estates, and a Baroque cathedral built by the then Protestant Estates. The Ingeborg Bachmann Prize for literature is awarded there.
