klaipeda: Klaipėda lies on the Baltic Sea coast, in Lithuania Minor, at the mouth of the river Akmena-Danė, whose usually ice-free port gave the city its regional importance. The old town stands on the left bank of the Danė, and its streets form a rectangular network laid out in the 13th to 15th centuries, with half-timbered buildings that reflect its German past. The Curonian Spit lies across the water, and a small part of it, Smiltynė, belongs to the city. Settlement by Baltic tribes is said to date from as early as the 7th century, when the Balts used the site as a trading centre for goods and annual fairs with the Germans.

In the 1240s, after Grand Duke Mindaugas of Lithuania accepted Christianity, crusaders moved into Sambia and founded a fort, Memelburg, in 1252. Its founding documents were signed on 29 July and 1 August 1252. In the 13th to 15th centuries the settlement was attacked by Sambians and Samogitians and burned or ruined about 20 times.

In 1525 it adopted Lutheranism when the Duchy of Prussia was created as a fief of the Polish crown, beginning a long period of prosperity for the port, which exported wheat from Lithuania through the mouth of the Neman. Sweden occupied the town at times between 1629 and 1635. In 1701 it became part of the Kingdom of Prussia and was one of its strongest fortresses. Russia held it from 1757 to 1762, and after Germany's unification in 1871 it was the German Empire's northernmost city.

Under the Treaty of Versailles the Klaipėda Region was detached from Germany and placed under French administration. Lithuanians staged the Klaipėda Revolt in January 1923, presenting the Entente with a fait accompli, and the League of Nations accepted the transfer in February 1923. The Klaipėda Convention of 8 May 1924 secured the region extensive autonomy. Nazi Germany annexed it in 1939. The Soviet Red Army took the nearly empty city on 28 January 1945, when only about 50 people remained, and the region was incorporated into the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic.

Klaipėda is the third-largest city of Lithuania and its only major seaport, the busiest in the Baltic states. It was named Memel officially from 1252 to 1923 and again from 1939 to 1945, and both names were in official use between 1923 and 1939. The Lithuanian name has been used since 1945. Its old town is known for its half-timbered fachwerk architecture, and the Lithuanian Sea Museum stands in the old Prussian star fort at Kopgalis.
kobayakawa-clan: The Kobayakawa claimed descent from the Taira clan, through its Kanmu-Heishi branch, which traced itself to Emperor Kanmu, the 50th emperor of Japan. Nakamura Munehira, son of Taira no Tsunemune, founded the Nakamura clan of Sagami Province. His second son, Dohi Sanehira, who died in 1191, founded the Dohi clan, and Sanehira's second son, Kobayakawa Tohira, who died in 1237, founded the Kobayakawa. Two sons of the third head of the family, Kobayakawa Shigehira, who died in 1264, divided the clan: Masahira, his third son, made his base at Numata and began the Numata-Kobayakawa, and Masakage, his fourth son, settled at Takehara and began the Takehara-Kobayakawa.

The two branches continued side by side for some three centuries; the lists of their heads end with the same man, Kobayakawa Takakage, born in 1533, the third son of Mōri Motonari. Takakage was the uncle of Mōri Terumoto, and his brother headed the allied Kikkawa clan, so that the Kobayakawa held great power in the politics of western Japan. Toyotomi Hideyoshi regarded Takakage as one of the best statesmen and appointed him to the Council of Five Elders, but Takakage died in 1597, before Hideyoshi.

At the end of the 16th century the Kobayakawa fought beside the Kikkawa, Mōri, Toyotomi and Ōtomo clans against the Shimazu for control of Kyūshū, and after the defeat of the Shimazu they were awarded Chikuzen Province as their fief. Takakage's successor, Kobayakawa Hideaki, born in 1582, was a nephew of Hideyoshi.

A powerful clan of the Sengoku period, the Kobayakawa were disbanded in the Edo period, after the Battle of Sekigahara. In the Meiji period the Mōri clan restored the house, which was given the title of baron in the new nobility. The Kusai clan of Takehara, a branch of the Kobayakawa, was also granted noble rank.
kobe: Kobe lies on the north shore of Osaka Bay in the Kansai region of Honshu, about 35 km west of Osaka and 70 km south-west of Kyoto. Wedged between the coast and the mountains, it is long and narrow, with Mount Rokko, 931 metres high, overlooking it. The shape of the coast at Wada Cape led to the development of a port, which has remained the economic centre of the city. The name comes from kamube, later kanbe, an archaic word for those who supported the city's Ikuta Shrine.

In the Nara and Heian periods the port was known as Owada Anchorage and was one of those from which imperial embassies were sent to China. In 1180 Taira no Kiyomori moved his grandson, Emperor Antoku, to Fukuhara-kyo in present-day Hyogo Ward, and the city was briefly the capital for about five months. In 1184 the Genpei War battle of Ichi-no-Tani was fought at the Taira fortress and the Ikuta Shrine, and the Minamoto prevailed. In the Kamakura period the port grew into a hub of trade with China and other countries and was known as Hyogo Port.

For most of its history the area was not a single political entity. Hyogo Port was opened to foreign trade, together with Osaka, on 1 January 1868, just before the Boshin War and the Meiji Restoration. Soon afterwards, in the Kobe Incident, troops from Bizen wounded several Western soldiers with gunfire. Many foreign residences from the period remain in the Kitano district. Kobe in its present form was founded on 1 April 1889.

On 16 and 17 March 1945 B-29 bombers attacked Kobe with incendiary bombs, killing 8,841 residents and destroying 21 percent of the urban area. On 17 January 1995 a magnitude 6.9 earthquake killed about 6,434 people in the city, made 212,443 homeless and toppled sections of the Hanshin Expressway.

Kobe is the capital of Hyogo Prefecture, with about 1.5 million people, and part of the Keihanshin metropolitan area with Osaka and Kyoto. Its port is one of Japan's busiest container ports. The city keeps a cosmopolitan character, with Western-style ijinkan residences in Kitano and Japan's first mosque, built in 1935. It is known for Kobe beef, the Arima Onsen hot springs and sake from the Nada district.
koblenz: Koblenz lies in a narrow flood plain between high hill ranges, where the Moselle meets the Middle Rhine. Its name comes from the Latin ad confluentes, meaning at the confluence. The meeting point of the rivers is the German Corner, which carries an equestrian statue of Emperor William I as a symbol of the unification of Germany. On the opposite bank of the Rhine the hill of Ehrenbreitstein bore early fortifications around 1000 BCE and is crowned today by a citadel.

In 55 BCE Roman troops under Julius Caesar reached the Rhine and built a bridge between Koblenz and Andernach. The military post Castellum apud Confluentes was one of those set up by Drusus. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the city was conquered by the Franks and became a royal seat, and Carolingian heirs met there to discuss what became the Treaty of Verdun in 843, by which it passed to Lotharingia. A synod of 922 condemned slavery. The Norsemen sacked the city in 882. In 1018 Emperor Henry II gave it to the archbishop-elector of Trier, whose successors held it until the end of the 18th century.

After the fall of the Bastille in 1789 the archbishop-elector, uncle of Louis XVI, welcomed French royalist émigrés, among them the Count of Provence and the Count of Artois. The Prince of Condé formed an army of aristocrats there. In 1792 the Duke of Brunswick began to march from Koblenz in an unsuccessful invasion of France, and the French Revolutionary army took the city in 1794. The Treaty of Lunéville of 1801 made it the capital of the French department of Rhin-et-Moselle. The Congress of Vienna assigned it to Prussia, and in 1822 it became the seat of government of the Prussian Rhine Province.

Koblenz is a city of Rhineland-Palatinate. The city was heavily bombed in the Second World War and rebuilt, and it served as the seat of government of Rhineland-Palatinate from 1947 to 1950. The Rhine Gorge was declared a World Heritage Site in 2002, with Koblenz marking its northern end. The city marked its 2,000th anniversary in 1992.
kochi: Kochi, formerly Cochin, lies on the south-west coast of India, bordering the Laccadive Sea, in the district of Ernakulam in Kerala. The city straddles the backwaters and takes in the northern end of a peninsula, several islands and part of the mainland. Much of it lies at sea level. The name is thought to come from the Malayalam kochu azhi, meaning small lagoon. Arab merchants called the place Kashi, and the Cochin Jewish community called it Kogin. The city reverted to its original Malayalam form Kochi in 1996.

Muziris, a port north of Kochi mostly identified with Kodungallur, was the centre of the Indian spice trade for many centuries. Kochi became a significant trading centre after the massive flooding of the Periyar in 1341 destroyed Muziris. The earliest documented references to Kochi are in the writings of the Chinese voyager Ma Huan, who visited in the 15th century with Admiral Zheng He's treasure fleet, and in the accounts of the Italian traveller Niccolò Da Conti, who visited in 1440. The Chinese fishing nets that are a symbol of the city were introduced by the Chinese in the 14th century.

The ruler of Perumpadappu fled to Kodungallur after the Zamorin of Calicut annexed the Ponnani region, and his family later moved to Kochi and established the Kingdom of Cochin. When Vasco da Gama landed at Kozhikode and the Zamorin fought the Portuguese, the ruler of Cochin aligned with the Portuguese. From 1503 to 1663 the Portuguese held Fort Emmanuel, before the Dutch took it over, and the Dutch later ceded the area to the United Kingdom. The construction of the Cochin Port and the reclamation of Willingdon Island in 1928 made Kochi a major seaport.

Kochi is a port city and the financial, industrial and commercial centre of Kerala, with 677,381 inhabitants in the municipal corporation at the 2011 census. It is the seat of the High Court of Kerala. Cochin Shipyard is the largest shipbuilding and maintenance facility in India in terms of capacity. The city once had a large Jewish community, known as the Malabar Yehuden and now increasingly as the Cochin Jews, who owned several synagogues. Landmarks include Mattanchery Palace and the Church of Saint Francis.
kolkata: Kolkata lies on the eastern bank of the Hooghly River in the lower Ganges Delta, at an elevation of 1.5 to 9 metres. Much of the city was originally a wetland, reclaimed over the decades to accommodate a growing population. Excavations at Chandraketugarh, 35 kilometres to the north, show that the region has been inhabited for over two millennia. The name derives from Kôlikata, the Bengali name of one of three villages that predated the British, the others being Sutanuti and Govindapur. One explanation is that it varies Kalikshetra, the area of the goddess Kali.

The earliest mention of the village of Kalikata is in Bipradas Pipilai's Manasa Vijay of 1495. The three villages were part of an estate belonging to the Sabarna Roy Choudhury family of zamindars, sold to the East India Company in 1698. The city's recorded history began in 1690 with the arrival of the Company. Job Charnock is often regarded as its founder, but in 2003 the Calcutta High Court ruled, in response to a petition, that the city has no founder.

The Company developed the area into Fort William. Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah occupied the fort in 1756 but was defeated at the Battle of Plassey in 1757. Under Company and then crown rule Calcutta was the de facto capital of India until 1911 and, after London, the second largest city of the British Empire. It was the centre of bureaucracy, politics, law, education, science and the arts, was associated with the Bengali Renaissance and was a hotbed of the Indian nationalist movement. The first newspaper in India, the Bengal Gazette, began publishing there in 1780.

The partition of Bengal in 1947 affected the city's fortunes, and Hindu refugees from East Bengal arrived in the following decades. In 1971 it hosted Bangladesh's government-in-exile. Its official name, Calcutta, was changed to Kolkata in 2001.

Kolkata is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of West Bengal, with a city population of about 4.5 million and a metropolitan area of over 15 million. Its landmarks include the Victoria Memorial and the Howrah Bridge. The University of Calcutta was the first modern university in South Asia, and the Port of Kolkata is India's oldest operating port. The city's celebrations of the festival of Durga Puja are recognised by UNESCO.
konrad-adenauer: Konrad Adenauer was born on 5 January 1876 in Cologne, in Rhenish Prussia, the third of five children of Johann Konrad Adenauer and Helene Scharfenberg. A formative influence was the Kulturkampf, the struggle of the Prussian state with the Catholic church, which left him with a lifelong dislike of Prussianism, as it did many Catholic Rhinelanders. A devout Catholic, he joined the Centre Party in 1906 and was elected to Cologne's city government the same year. In 1909 he became vice-mayor, and in 1917 he was unanimously elected Mayor of Cologne for twelve years, re-elected in 1929.

Adenauer opposed Adolf Hitler and the Nazis, but in the early 1930s he thought they should be brought into the Prussian and Reich governments. The Nazis came to power on 30 January 1933, and his term as mayor ended that year. After the war the American army reinstalled him as Mayor of Cologne, but when the city passed into the British zone, General Gerald Templer dismissed him for incompetence in December 1945. The dismissal helped his later career, since he could pursue alliance with the Allies without being called a sell-out. From 1946 to 1966 he led the Christian Democratic Union.

The first Bundestag election, on 15 August 1949, made the Christian Democrats the strongest party, and Adenauer became chancellor. His rival, the Social Democrat Kurt Schumacher, wanted a united, socialist and neutral Germany; Adenauer preferred integration with Western states, especially France and the United States, even at the price of continued division. West Germany joined NATO, and the Bundeswehr was established in 1955 and 1956. He refused to recognise East Germany or the Oder-Neisse line as Poland's frontier. In 1957 he signed the Treaty of Rome, and from 1958 he built a close friendship with Charles de Gaulle. In 1961 the Berlin Wall was built, and his relationship with John F. Kennedy was strained.

Adenauer resigned as chancellor at 87 and led the CDU until he was 90, and he was often called Der Alte, the old one. He died on 19 April 1967, aged 91, at his home in Rhöndorf. His requiem mass in Cologne Cathedral was attended by guests from over a hundred countries and organisations, and he is buried at Rhöndorf. He is considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union.
konya: Konya stands on the south-western edge of the Central Anatolian Plateau. It was known as Iconium in antiquity and into Seljuk times, in Greek Ikónion, and the Rum Seljuks called it Dârülmülk. The name is believed to correspond to Ikkuwaniya, a Late Bronze Age place known from Hittite records.

The region has been inhabited since the third millennium BCE, and excavations show settlement in the Late Copper Age, around 3000 BCE. It fell at different times to the Hittites, the Phrygians, the Persians and the Romans, and Xenophon describes Iconium as the last city of Phrygia. After Alexander the Great defeated Darius III in 333 BCE, the town came under Seleucus I Nicator, and later under the kings of Pergamon. Under the emperor Claudius it was renamed Claudiconium, and under Hadrian it was Colonia Aelia Hadriana.

Paul and Silas probably visited it around 50 CE, and the apocryphal Acts of Paul and Thecla make it the birthplace of Saint Thecla. Under the Byzantine Empire it became a bishop's seat and, around 370, a metropolitan see for Lycaonia.

From the eighth to the tenth century it was a frequent target of Arab attacks. The Seljuk Turks conquered it in the 11th century, and it became the capital of their Sultanate of Rum. It was briefly occupied by the army of the First Crusade in 1097 and by Frederick Barbarossa in 1190. Konya reached the height of its wealth and influence in the second half of the 12th century, when the sultans subdued the Danishmend beyliks and took ports on the Mediterranean and Black Sea.

After the sultanate fell, the Karamanids took Konya, and in 1420 their beylik fell to the Ottoman Empire. Under Ottoman rule it was governed by the sultans' sons and was the capital of the Karaman Eyalet until 1864. İbrahim Paşa occupied it in 1832, and it went into decline afterwards.

Konya is a major city of central Turkey and the capital of Konya Province. It was the last home of Rumi, whose turquoise-domed tomb is its main tourist attraction. In 1273 his followers established the Mevlevi order, known as the Whirling Dervishes, and Konya is its spiritual centre.
korce: Korçë stands on a plateau some 850 m above sea level, surrounded by the Morava Mountains. The current name is of Slavic origin: gorica means hill in the South Slavic languages and is a very common toponym. The city is known by other names, among them Goritsa in Bulgarian, Macedonian and Serbian, Korytsa in Greek, Coriza in Italian and Görice in Turkish. The Old Bazaar, with the Mirahori Mosque, is regarded as the urban core, and the town's actual physiognomy was realised in the 19th century.

Korçë's foundation is closely tied to Ilias Bey Mirahori, an Albanian convert to Islam, Master of the Stables to Sultan Bayezid II. In 1484 the Sultan rewarded him with seven villages in the Korçë area, and a series of firmans replaced these in 1497 with the locality of Piskopiye, whose boundaries correspond to the territory of today's city. When the nearby town of Moscopole was destroyed by Ali Pasha's men in 1769, some of its commerce moved to Korçë, and part of its population came from there. Greek schools were founded from 1724, and on the eve of the Balkan Wars 2,115 students attended Greek education in the city.

Ottoman rule lasted until 1912, when Albania declared its independence. Armed Albanian bands under Sali Butka, Spiro Bellkameni and Kajo Babjeni briefly liberated Korçë in August 1912. Because of its proximity to Greece, the city was fiercely contested in the Balkan Wars, and Greek forces captured it on 6 December 1912. After 1916 the city came under French control, which lasted until 1920. Albanian bands led by Themistokli Gërmenji and Sali Butka fought for Albanian self-administration against the Venizelist forces.

Korçë is the seat of Korçë County in south-eastern Albania, with 51,152 inhabitants in the city at the 2011 census. It has been regarded as the intellectual capital of southern Albania. Fan Noli University was founded in 1971, and the National Museum of Medieval Art holds about 7,000 icons. Aromanian and Greek communities remain, and the largest carnival in Albania takes place there before Orthodox Easter.
korea: Korea consists of the Korean Peninsula, Jeju Island and smaller islands in East Asia. The peninsula extends southward about 1,100 km from the continent, between the Sea of Japan to the east and the Yellow Sea to the west, and the Korea Strait lies between it and Japan. The Amnok (Yalu) River separates it from China in the northwest and the Duman (Tumen) River from China and Russia in the northeast. The name Korea is a modern spelling of Corea, attested in English from 1614, which comes from the kingdom of Goryeo.

According to Korean legend, Dangun founded Gojoseon in 2333 BCE. The Han dynasty defeated it in 108 BCE and installed four commanderies in the north, and Goguryeo annexed them all by 313. In the Three Kingdoms period Goguryeo held the north and Manchuria, while Baekje and Silla held the south. Silla allied with the Tang dynasty in the 640s to conquer Baekje and Goguryeo and drove the Tang from the peninsula in 676. Goryeo, founded in 918, replaced Silla, and in the 13th century it became a vassal state of the Mongol Empire.

In 1392 General Yi Seong-gye overthrew Goryeo and founded the Joseon dynasty, with its capital at Hanseong, now Seoul, and in 1394 he adopted Confucianism as the official ideology. The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was created in the 15th century. Japanese and Qing invasions later devastated Joseon. After Japan's victory in the First Sino-Japanese War in 1895, China lost suzerainty over Korea, and in 1897 Joseon became the Korean Empire. Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910. In 1945 Soviet and American zones were set at the 38th parallel, two governments were established in 1948, and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953, in which more than 1.2 million people died, ended in an armistice.

Korea is divided between North Korea and South Korea, with a demilitarized zone approximating the original partition. Korean is the official language of both and is written almost entirely in Hangul. Confucian tradition has dominated Korean thought, alongside Buddhism, Taoism and Korean Shamanism. Surviving works of its early history include Cheomseongdae, an astronomical observatory built in 634, and the Great Dharani Sutra, the earliest known surviving Korean woodblock printing, believed to date from 750-51.
korean-war: Korea had been a colony of the Empire of Japan from 1910 to 1945. As the Second World War drew to a close, two American colonels, Dean Rusk and Charles H. Bonesteel III, chose the 38th parallel on 11 August 1945 as the line dividing the peninsula into a Soviet and an American occupation zone. The zones formed their own governments in 1948: North Korea under Kim Il Sung in Pyongyang and South Korea under Syngman Rhee in Seoul, each claiming to be the only legitimate government of all Korea. Border clashes were extensive, and Kim Il Sung began seeking Stalin's support for an invasion in March 1949.

On 25 June 1950 the Korean People's Army crossed the 38th parallel behind artillery fire, with tanks against a South Korean army that had none. The UN Security Council denounced the invasion the same day; the Soviet representative, whose government was boycotting the council, was absent and could not veto. UN forces comprised 21 countries, with the United States providing around 90 per cent of the military personnel. Seoul fell on 28 June, and by early August the South Korean army and its allies held only the Pusan Perimeter in the south-east.

On 15 September UN forces landed at Incheon, well behind the North Korean lines, and broke out of the perimeter soon afterwards. They retook Seoul and invaded North Korea in October. On 19 October the Chinese People's Volunteer Army crossed the Yalu and entered the war. Chinese and North Korean forces took Seoul a second time on 4 January 1951, before a UN counter-offensive regained it two months later. The fighting then became a war of attrition with little change of territory, while armistice talks began on 10 July 1951 and were delayed for two years by the repatriation of prisoners of war. Throughout, the United Nations Command bombed North Korea.

Combat ended on 27 July 1953 with the signing of the Korean Armistice Agreement, which allowed the exchange of prisoners and created a demilitarised zone four kilometres wide along the front line. The war caused around one million military deaths and an estimated 1.5 million to 3 million civilian deaths. Alleged war crimes include the mass killing of alleged communists by South Korea, the Seoul National University Hospital massacre by North Korea and the carpet bombing of North Korea by the United Nations Command. No peace treaty has been signed. The war saw armoured offensives, tunnel warfare by Chinese forces and the first large jet aircraft battles.
kosovo: Kosovo covers 10,887 km2 in the centre of Southeast Europe. Most of its borders run along mountains, notably the Accursed Mountains in the west, a continuation of the Dinaric Alps, and the Šar Mountains in the southeast. Between them lie two major plains, the Kosovo Plain in the east and the Metohija Plain in the west. The name comes from Kosovo Polje, Blackbird Field, the karst field where the Battle of Kosovo was fought in 1389. In the Middle Ages the western territory was called Metohija, because large portions of land belonged to Serbian Orthodox monasteries and Mount Athos; Albanians call it Dukagjini.

The earliest evidence of organised settlement belongs to the Neolithic Starčevo and Vinča cultures. In antiquity the area was the core of Dardania, named after the Dardani, a Paleo-Balkan people usually described as Illyrian, though scholars debate whether they were Illyrian or Thracian. Dardania was incorporated into the Roman Empire in the 1st century BCE and became a separate Roman province in the 3rd century CE. Under the Byzantines the region faced Slavic migrations in the 6th and 7th centuries, and control passed between the Byzantines and the First Bulgarian Empire.

In the 13th century Kosovo became integral to the medieval Serbian state and the establishment of the Serbian Patriarchate. Ottoman expansion in the late 14th and 15th centuries brought the fall of the Serbian Empire, and the Battle of Kosovo of 1389, in which a Serbian-led coalition fought the Ottoman Empire, is regarded as one of its defining moments. Various dynasties, chiefly the Branković, governed afterwards. The Ottoman Empire fully conquered Kosovo after the Second Battle of Kosovo and ruled for nearly five centuries until 1912. The Ottoman Vilayet of Kosovo, created in 1877, was the first time the name was applied to a wider area.

Kosovo was a centre of the Albanian Renaissance and saw Albanian revolts in 1910 and 1912. After the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 it was ceded to the Kingdom of Serbia, and after the Second World War it became an Autonomous Province within Yugoslavia. Tensions between the Albanian and Serb communities culminated in the Kosovo War of 1998 and 1999, after which the Yugoslav Army withdrew and the United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo was established.

Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia on 17 February 2008. Its recognition is partial, and Serbia does not officially recognise it as a state. The capital and largest city is Pristina, and the euro is the official currency. Four Serbian Orthodox churches and monasteries, including Visoki Dečani, the Patriarchate of Peja, Our Lady of Ljeviš and Gračanica, are inscribed as the World Heritage Site Medieval Monuments in Kosovo.
krakow: Kraków lies in southern Poland on the Vistula river, about 219 metres above sea level, on the border between several physiographic regions: the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland to the north-west, the Małopolska Upland to the north-east, the Sandomierz Basin to the east and the foothills of the Carpathians to the south. Its name is traditionally derived from Krakus, the founder and ruler of the Vistulans in tradition, though historians dispute the true origin and the name may come from kruk, meaning crow or raven.

Settlement on the site of Wawel Castle goes back to the Stone Age. Kraków began as a fortified settlement of the Vistulans, a Lechitic tribe, around the 8th century. A legend says Krakus built it above a cave occupied by a dragon, Smok Wawelski. It was a notable commercial centre controlled by Moravia and then captured by the Bohemian duke Boleslaus I in 955, and Mieszko I, the first acclaimed ruler of Poland, took it from the Bohemians towards the end of his reign. In 1038 it became the seat of the Piast monarchs, and it remained the centre of administration until the late 16th century, when Sigismund III Vasa moved his court to Warsaw.

The 15th and 16th centuries were Poland's Golden Age, and many works of Renaissance art and architecture were created in Kraków, including the synagogues of Kazimierz. In 1473 Kasper Straube printed the Calendarium Cracoviense there, the first work printed in Poland. In 1794 Tadeusz Kościuszko began an unsuccessful insurrection in the Main Square; it led to the third and final partition of Poland, and Kraków came under Habsburg rule. After the Second Polish Republic emerged in 1918, the city became again a major academic and cultural centre. In the Second World War it became the seat of Nazi Germany's General Government, and its Jewish population was forced into the Kraków Ghetto and sent to extermination camps. The city was spared destruction.

Kraków is the second-largest city in Poland, with 816,614 inhabitants, and was its official capital until 1596. Its Old Town, with the nearby Wieliczka Salt Mine, is among Poland's first World Heritage Sites, declared in 1978. Landmarks include Wawel Cathedral and Wawel Castle, St Mary's Basilica and Rynek Główny, the largest medieval market square in Europe. Jagiellonian University, founded in 1364 as the Studium Generale, is the oldest university in Poland. Karol Wojtyła, archbishop of Kraków, became Pope John Paul II in 1978.
krasnodar: Krasnodar stands on the right bank of the Kuban River, about 1,300 km south of Moscow, with the Black Sea 120 km to the west. The climate is humid subtropical. Winters are cold and damp with unstable snow cover, the July average is 24.1 °C, and about 735 millimetres of rain and snow fall in a year. No mountains shield the city from cold waves, so winter temperatures below −20 °C are not uncommon.

The city began in 1793 as a military camp and then a fortress built by the Black Sea Cossacks to defend the imperial borders and to assert Russian dominion over Circassia, a claim that Ottoman Turkey contested. Its name, Yekaterinodar, meant Catherine's Gift, recognising both Catherine the Great's grant of land in the Kuban to the Cossacks and Saint Catherine of Alexandria, regarded as the city's patron. It received town status in 1867 and by 1888 had about 45,000 people. The 1897 census counted 65,606, of whom 52.9 per cent spoke Russian and 38.3 per cent Ukrainian.

During the Russian Civil War the city changed hands several times between the Red Army and the Volunteer Army. The White general Lavr Kornilov besieged it on 10 April 1918 and was killed a week later when a Bolshevik shell destroyed the farmhouse that served as his headquarters. On 7 December 1920 it was renamed Krasnodar, meaning Gift of the Reds. The city lost over 14 per cent of its population in the Soviet famine of 1932–1933.

German forces occupied Krasnodar from 9 August 1942 to 12 February 1943. The city was heavily damaged, and the Gestapo and mobile SS execution squads killed thousands of Jews, Communists and suspected partisans. From 14 to 17 July 1943 a Soviet tribunal at Krasnodar tried people for collaboration and war crimes and pronounced eight death sentences, carried out in the city square before a crowd of about thirty thousand.

Krasnodar is the largest city and administrative centre of Krasnodar Krai, with a population of 1,154,885 within the city limits. The 2021 census counted one million people there for the first time. The historic centre keeps buildings from the 19th century, and the city has St Catherine's Cathedral and a steel lattice hyperboloid tower built by the engineer Vladimir Shukhov in 1928. It is the home of the Kuban Cossack Choir and of the Kovalenko Krasnodar Regional Art Museum, the oldest public art museum in the North Caucasus.
krishna: The tradition of Krishna appears to have grown from the merging of several independent deities of ancient India, the earliest attested being Vāsudeva, a hero-god of the Vrishni tribe, whose worship is attested from the 5th to 6th centuries BCE in the writings of Pāṇini and from the 2nd century BCE in inscriptions such as the Heliodorus pillar. The Vrishnis were later thought to have merged with the Yadavas, whose hero-god was Krishna, and the two deities became one, who was identified with Vishnu in the Mahabharata. Around 180 BCE the Indo-Greek king Agathocles issued coins whose images are now read as Balarama and Vāsudeva-Krishna. The Mahabharata is the earliest text to describe Krishna as a personality in detail.

Hindus worship Krishna as the eighth avatar of Vishnu and, in Krishnaite traditions, as the Supreme God. His name is a Sanskrit word meaning black, dark or dark blue, and he is usually shown with dark or blue skin. The Mahabharata, the Harivamsa, the Bhagavata Purana and the Vishnu Purana tell his life, and agree on the main story. He is born in a prison at Mathura to Devaki and Vasudeva and raised by Nanda and Yashoda, because Devaki's brother, the tyrant Kamsa, has been told that her eighth child will kill him. As a boy he is a cowherd and a prankster, the butter thief, who lifts Govardhana hill to shelter Vrindavana from rain.

As an adult he kills Kamsa and leads the Yadavas to the city of Dwaraka. In the Kurukshetra War he serves as Arjuna's charioteer on condition that he raise no weapon, and his counsel to Arjuna forms the Bhagavad Gita.

Krishna is a central figure of bhakti, devotional worship, within Vaishnavism, and devotees see lila, divine play, as the central principle of the universe. His birth is observed each year at Krishna Janmashtami, in late August or early September, with fasting, singing, night vigils and temple visits. Mathura and Vrindavan, where there are about 5,500 temples, are major pilgrimage sites, and regional forms include Jagannatha in Odisha, Vithoba in Maharashtra and Guruvayoorappan in Kerala. His stories inspired dance forms such as Bharatanatyam, Kathakali and Odissi, and reliefs at Prambanan in Java, dated to the 9th century, show episodes of his life.
kuala-lumpur: Kuala Lumpur lies in the Klang Valley, bordered by the Titiwangsa Mountains in the east and the Strait of Malacca in the west. It stands at the confluence of the Klang and Gombak rivers, in the centre of Selangor on the central west coast of Peninsular Malaysia. The municipality covers 243 square kilometres, and its highest point is Bukit Nanas at 94 metres.

The name means muddy confluence in Malay, from kuala, the point where two rivers join, and lumpur, mud. Its origin is uncertain. One suggestion is that it was named after a Sungai Lumpur, a muddy river. Others propose Pengkalan Lumpur, muddy landing place, or a Cantonese word, lam-pa, for flooded jungle, but there is no firm contemporary evidence for these.

Kuala Lumpur was first developed around 1857 by Raja Abdullah as a town serving the tin mines of the region. Yap Ah Loy and Frank Swettenham were instrumental in its early development in the late 19th century. In 1872 Swettenham described the settlement beside the Klang River as a purely Chinese village, though a Malay stockade already stood at Bukit Nanas. It was the capital of Selangor from 1880 until 1978. Most of its notable colonial-era buildings date from the end of the 19th century and the early 20th, among them the railway station and the Jamek Mosque.

The city belonged to the Federated Malay States from the late 19th century, was under the Empire of Japan from 1942 to 1945, and became part of the Malayan Union in 1946 and the Federation of Malaya in 1948. It was the founding capital of the Federation of Malaya and of Malaysia, formed in 1963. It received city status in 1972, and in 1974 it was separated from Selangor to become the first Federal Territory. Its federal executive and judicial branches moved to Putrajaya in early 1999.

Kuala Lumpur is the capital and most populous city of Malaysia, with 2,111,536 people. It is the seat of the Parliament of Malaysia and of the Istana Negara, the official residence of the monarch. Its population includes the Malays, Chinese and Indians as well as Eurasians, Kadazans, Ibans and other Indigenous peoples. The Petronas Towers are the tallest twin buildings in the world, and the University of Malaya, established in 1949, is the oldest university in Malaysia.
kuntillet-ajrud: Kuntillet Ajrud, also known by the Hebrew name Horvat Teman, was one of the few water sources along the Darb el-Ghazza, the Gaza Road, which ran from the site of ancient Eilat or Ezion-Geber past Kuntillet Ajrud and Kadesh Barnea up to Gaza. Carbon-14 dating indicates that the site was occupied from 801 to 770 BCE.

The main building is fortress-like and divided into two rooms, one large and one small, both with low benches. Both rooms held paintings and inscriptions on the walls and on two large water jars, or pithoi, one found in each room.

What the site was for is disputed. It is frequently described as a shrine, though this is not certain. The excavator, Ze'ev Meshel, first argued for a religious function from the inscriptions and drawings with religious themes and from an unusual amount of linen, which he connected with the dress of priests. Other scholars point out that the site has no temple, shrine or cultic objects, and that similar textiles have since been found at Kadesh Barnea. Four inscriptions carry the military title Commander of the Fortress, three on storage jars and one on the plastered walls, which supports the view that it was a state-sponsored fortress or a caravanserai.

Although its position in the Sinai would normally point to the Kingdom of Judah, the occupants are usually taken to have come from the northern Kingdom of Israel. The evidence is the pottery, the personal names with the ending -yaw, the northern spelling of some inscriptions and the references to Yahweh of Samaria.

Edward Henry Palmer identified the place in 1869, when it was known as Contellet Garaiyeh, with the station Gypsaria on the Tabula Peutingeriana, and noted the remains of an ancient fort. Ze'ev Meshel of Tel Aviv University excavated it in 1975 and 1976, and the excavation report was published in 2012.

The paintings on the pithoi show animals, stylised trees and human figures. They appear to have been made over a considerable period by several artists and form no coherent scenes. Talley Ornan has argued that all the drawings have parallels in Neo-Assyrian palace reliefs and were preliminary sketches for wall paintings, and Schniedewind has read the inscriptions as scribal exercises of soldiers stationed at the fortress. Mordechai Gilula's theory that two figures on one jar represent Yahweh and the goddess Asherah has been almost abandoned: the scholars who have analysed the images in most detail hold that they are Bes or Bes-like figures.
kwame-nkrumah: Kwame Nkrumah was born Francis Nwia Kofi Nkrumah on 21 September 1909 at Nkroful, a small village in the Nzema area of the southwest Gold Coast, close to the frontier with the French colony of the Ivory Coast. He was his mother's only child. His father, a goldsmith, worked at Half Assini, and Nkrumah went to the elementary school run there by a Catholic mission. After ten years in the United States he returned to London in May 1945 and enrolled at the London School of Economics, then at University College London, where his supervisor A. J. Ayer thought he lacked an analytical mind, and he did not complete his law studies at Gray's Inn.

The Gold Coast constitution of 1946 gave Africans a majority on the legislative council for the first time, and the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC), the colony's first true political party, was founded in August 1947. It hired Nkrumah to run it, and he sailed home from Liverpool in November 1947. In April 1949 his supporters pressed him to leave the UGCC, and on 12 June 1949 he announced the Convention People's Party (CPP), choosing the word convention, he said, to carry the masses with us. He became prime minister in 1952 and worked closely with the British governor, Arden-Clarke, who told the civil service to support the new government.

Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957, the first British African colony to gain majority-rule independence, and the celebrations in Accra drew over 100 reporters and photographers. His government was socialist and nationalist and funded industrial and energy projects. Accra hosted a series of pan-African meetings: the First Conference of Independent States in April 1958 and the All-African Peoples' Conference in December 1958, with representatives of 62 nationalist organisations.

Unrest followed independence, and in December 1957 an act banned regional or tribal political parties; opposition parties then formed the United Party under Kofi Abrefa Busia. After an alleged assassination plot and worsening economic conditions Nkrumah's government became more authoritarian, and in 1964 a constitutional amendment made Ghana a one-party state with Nkrumah as president for life. While he was on a state visit to China in February 1966, the National Liberation Council, led by Joseph Arthur Ankrah, overthrew him in a coup. He lived the rest of his life in Conakry, Guinea, and died in Bucharest on 27 April 1972. He is remembered as a leading advocate of pan-Africanism and a founding member of the Organisation of African Unity.
kyiv: Kyiv lies on both banks of the Dnieper River, which flows southward through the city toward the Black Sea. The older and higher western part sits on wooded hills with ravines and small rivers, and these gave the city toponyms such as Podil (lower), Pechersk (caves) and uzviz (a steep street). The city expanded onto the low left bank to the east only in the 20th century. Its name is traditionally derived from Kyi, one of four founders named in tradition, though the linguist Jaroslav Rudnyckyj reads it as meaning palisaded settlement.

The first people in the region lived there in the late Paleolithic. Roman coins of the 2nd to 4th centuries suggest trade with the eastern provinces of the Roman Empire. Scholars debate when the city was founded. The traditional date is 482 CE, so the city marked its 1,500th anniversary in 1982, while archaeology points to the sixth or seventh century, and some researchers date it as late as the late 9th century. In the Primary Chronicle the brothers Kyi, Shchek and Khoryv and their sister Lybid are the founders.

A Slavic settlement on the trade route between Scandinavia and Constantinople, it was a tributary of the Khazars until its capture by the Varangians in the mid-9th century. Under Varangian rule it became a capital of Kievan Rus', the first East Slavic state. The Siege of Kiev in 1240 left it in ruins, and it lost most of its influence for centuries. It grew into a centre of Eastern Orthodox learning in the 16th century, and the Mohyla Academy was founded as a theological school in 1632.

The city prospered during the Industrial Revolution of the Russian Empire in the late 19th century. In 1918 the Ukrainian People's Republic declared independence and made Kyiv its capital. After the Ukrainian-Soviet and Polish-Soviet wars it became part of the Ukrainian SSR, whose capital it became in 1934. It suffered significant destruction in World War II and recovered as the third-largest city of the Soviet Union. It became the capital of independent Ukraine in 1991.

Kyiv is the capital and most populous city of Ukraine, with 2,952,301 inhabitants in January 2022. It has a special legal status as a city that is also treated as a region of the country. It remains a centre of Eastern Orthodox Christianity, and the Saint Sophia Cathedral and the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, the Monastery of the Caves, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Taras Shevchenko University, founded in 1834, is the oldest university in continuous operation there.
kyushu: Kyushu is the most southerly of Japan's four main islands, with a land area of 36,782 km2. It is mountainous, and its highest point is Mount Kujū at 1,791 m. Mount Aso, at 1,591 m, is the largest active volcano in Japan, and tectonic activity also shows in many hot springs, the best known of them at Beppu on the east shore and around Aso in the centre. The Kanmon Straits separate the island from Honshu. Because it is the island nearest the Asian continent, it has historically been the gateway to Japan. Parts of Kyushu, particularly Miyazaki and Kagoshima prefectures, have a subtropical climate, and the main crops are rice, tea, tobacco, sweet potatoes and soy.

Kyushu has been called Kyūkoku, the Nine Countries, Chinzei, meaning West of the Pacified Area, and Tsukushi-no-shima. The historical region of Saikaidō, the West Sea Circuit, covered the island and its surroundings, and the present name Kyūshū, nine provinces, comes from the nine ancient provinces on it: Chikuzen, Chikugo, Hizen, Higo, Buzen, Bungo, Hyūga, Ōsumi and Satsuma. In the Taihō Code reforms of the 8th century, Dazaifu was established as a special administrative term for the region. One theory holds that in ancient times Kyushu was home to its own independent dynasty, with a southern-influenced culture and tradition distinct from that of Honshu.

Kyushu holds about 10 percent of Japan's population, concentrated along the northwest in Fukuoka and Kitakyushu, with corridors running to Sasebo, Nagasaki, Kumamoto and Kagoshima. It has maintained the strongest economic and cultural ties with Okinawa from ancient times, and traces of Okinawan scales, cuisine and language appear throughout. The gottan, a traditional stringed instrument, is regarded as a midpoint between the shamisen of mainland Japan and the Okinawan sanshin. Porcelain from Arita, Imari, Satsuma and Karatsu is well known, and the Tanegashima Space Center is Japan's largest rocket-launch complex. The island has World Heritage Sites including Yakushima, the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, and the Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region.
